title: Administration
text: # Administration Install and run your own MTL Explorer. To learn how to use the app, see the User guide . 1. Install and import a few test files. 2. Configure the login, data folders, and HTTPS. 3. Optional: connect Garmin or Google Health . 4. Check the map, routing, and search services . 5. Set up backups and updates . If something fails, see troubleshooting . Keep passwords, tracks, photos, health data, and backups private.

title: Configuration
text: # Configuration - Login and credentials - Data folders - HTTPS and reverse proxies - Environment settings

title: Login and credentials
text: # Login and credentials The default login is user mtl with password change-me. Change it before other people or the internet can reach MTL Explorer. Your login is set in a file called .env, next to docker-compose.yml: Create it on the machine that runs Docker, not inside the container or data/. 1. Create the file and allow only your user to read it. On macOS or Linux: On Windows PowerShell: 2. Add your login: 3. Apply it: Do not share or commit .env. To keep it somewhere else, pass it on every start and update: MTL Explorer serves plain HTTP on port 18080. For HTTPS, put a reverse proxy in front of it. ## Login reference Settings → Session shows a login reference (ClientLoginRef). If you report a problem, include it so the matching log entries can be found. It is not a password and cannot be used to sign in.

title: Environment settings
text: # Environment settings MTL Explorer reads its settings from .env, next to docker-compose.yml. Keep this file private. If you keep it somewhere else, start and update with docker compose --env-file /path/to/mtl.env .... | Setting | Purpose | | --- | --- | | MTL_USER_LOGIN, MTL_USER_PASSWORD | Your login | | MTL_POSTGRES_PASSWORD | Database password | | MTL_APP_IMAGE | Use a different app image | | MTL_BROUTER_IMAGE, MTL_LOCATION_SEARCH_IMAGE, MTL_MAP_IMAGE | Use different service images | | MTL_IMAGE_PULL_POLICY | When Docker downloads new images | | MTL_UPDATES_ENABLED, MTL_UPDATES_FEED_URL | Optional check for new releases | | MTL_GOOGLE_HEALTH_CLIENT_ID, MTL_GOOGLE_HEALTH_CLIENT_SECRET | Google Health connection | After changing .env, run docker compose up -d to apply it. The Compose file lists all settings and their defaults. Advanced server settings are in the server configuration . Do not post your .env or full configuration publicly; it contains passwords.

title: HTTPS and reverse proxies
text: # HTTPS and reverse proxies MTL Explorer serves plain HTTP on port 18080. To reach it securely from outside your home network, put a reverse proxy with HTTPS in front of it, such as Caddy, Traefik, or nginx. HTTP/1.1 is supported. HTTP/2 is optional. 1. Point your hostname to the app's port 18080. 2. Set up a valid certificate in the proxy. 3. Keep the /mtl/ path, and forward the original host and scheme (https). 4. Keep streaming and range requests working; photos, videos, and maps need them. 5. Allow long requests: planning a long route can take up to five minutes. 6. Open https://<your-host>/mtl/ and test the login, the map, a photo download, and route planning. If something does not load, check the browser console and the server logs for path or mixed-content errors. For Google Health, the connection uses a manual copy-and-paste step that works behind a proxy; see Google Health setup .

title: Data folders
text: # Data folders MTL Explorer keeps all its data in data/, next to docker-compose.yml: Copy GPS files into ./data/gpx/; MTL Explorer finds them automatically. Unzip ZIP archives first. Put photos and videos into ./data/media/. Keep the whole data/ folder when you update. Re-downloading maps and routing data takes a long time. ## Use other folders To keep your data or media somewhere else, edit the app.volumes section in docker-compose.yml. Change only the left side of each line: Put your tracks in /your/mtl-data/gpx. Keep gpx and google-health-staging inside the same folder; Google Health imports need them together. ## Fix permissions on Linux If Docker created ./data/ as root and imports fail, give it back to your user:

title: Garmin setup
text: # Garmin setup Garmin sync is optional and off by default. It downloads your Garmin activities into the GPS folder, where MTL Explorer imports them. 1. Create application.yml next to docker-compose.yml with your Garmin login: This file contains your password. Allow only your user to read it. 2. Create or extend compose.override.yml next to it. If it already has an app section, add these lines to it: Keep the existing ./data:/app/mtl-data line in docker-compose.yml. 3. Apply the changes: 4. Open Settings → Import & sync → Garmin → Sync now . Check Garmin command output , then wait until Settings → Processing is done. Some downloads can fail. MTL Explorer retries failed downloads in a different format, but not every error can be fixed this way. See Garmin export for how it works.

title: Google Health setup
text: # Google Health setup Google Health is an optional beta feature . It keeps a read-only copy of your Google Health data (exercise, sleep, activity, measurements, and heart rate) on your own server, and imports exercise routes as tracks. Errors and sync interruptions may occur. To use it, see the Health guide . This page covers setup. Before you start: - You need your own Google Cloud project with access to the Google Health API. Google decides who gets access, and its rules can change. Check Google's requirements first. - Your Google Account must be linked to an active Google Health profile. If needed, create one or move your Fitbit account in the Google Health mobile app; see Google's account requirements . - In Google's Testing mode, you must reconnect every seven days. Your stored data stays. - One Google account per MTL Explorer installation. Health data and route locations are sensitive. Protect the database, backups, login, and reverse proxy. Health data is stored in the database, and routes in ./data/gpx/google-health/. Back up ./data/postgis and ./data/gpx together. Without Google credentials, the feature simply stays unconfigured. To turn it off completely, set MTL_GOOGLE_HEALTH_ENABLED=false in .env. Each installation connects to Google directly, so your health data never passes through a third-party service. That is why every installation needs its own Google setup. ### One-time installation setup In MTL Explorer, open Settings → Import & sync → Google Health → Start setup . The setup assistant shows the scopes, an .env template, server checks, and links to each Google page: Cloud Console , API Library , Auth Platform , Audience , OAuth Clients , and Data Access . 1. Select a Google Cloud project and enable Google Health API . 2. Open Google Auth Platform . If Google shows Get started , fill in: - App name: enter MTL Explorer. - User support email: select your email, then select Next . - Audience: select External unless all users belong to the same Google Workspace organization, then select Next . - Contact Information: enter your email, then select Next . - Finish: accept the user-data policy, then select Continue and Create . 3. Open Audience . Check that the publishing status is Testing and the user type is External . Under Test users , select + Add users , enter the Google account that owns the health data, and select Save . Check that the account appears in the list. Google will warn that the app is unverified. This is expected. Keep the app in Testing : this is the supported setup. You don't need to publish the app or have it verified by Google. The only drawback is reconnecting once a week. 4. Open Clients and create an OAuth client: - Application type: select Desktop app . - Name: enter MTL Explorer. - Select Create , then Download JSON and save the file. - Before closing Google's dialog, copy the Client ID and Client secret. You need both in step 6. 5. Open Data Access , select Add or remove scopes , and add the four read-only scopes: Tip: Select Copy all four scopes in the assistant, paste them into Manually add scopes , then select Add to table , Update , and Save . The first three are required. Location is optional and only needed for exercise routes. 6. Add the client ID and secret to .env, next to docker-compose.yml. Create .env first if it is missing: Keep this secret. If you change it later, you must reconnect Google Health. Your stored health data stays. 7. Apply the change: Do not use docker compose restart; it does not load the new settings. Wait until MTL Explorer is back, sign in, return to the assistant, and select Check again . If you keep .env elsewhere, use docker compose --env-file "/path/to/mtl.env" up -d. On a NAS, add both settings to the stack environment and recreate the app container. Advanced: if MTL Explorer runs behind HTTPS and you prefer an automatic callback, set MTL_GOOGLE_HEALTH_REDIRECT_URI to its public HTTPS callback address and use a Web application OAuth client with exactly the same address. Leave it unset for the normal setup. See Google Health authorization for why the setup works this way. ### Connect the Google account 1. Open Settings → Import & sync → Google Health . 2. In the setup assistant, select Open Google consent . 3. On Google's Select what this app can access screen, select Select all and Continue . You can leave Location unchecked if you don't need exercise routes. 4. Google opens http://127.0.0.1:1/mtl-explorer-oauth and the browser shows an error. This is expected. Copy the complete address from the address bar. 5. Return to MTL Explorer, paste the address, and select Complete connection within ten minutes. 6. Select Open Health , or open Manage to review access. Follow the sync link to Processing to watch the first import. The last 24 hours appear first; the rest of the week and older history follow over time. Temporary errors are retried automatically. Settings → Processing shows what failed and when it is retried next. ### Reconnect When access is about to expire or has expired, Settings shows a message. Select Reauthorize , open Google consent, copy the new address, and paste it into MTL Explorer. Your Google setup and stored data stay unchanged. ### Diagnose Google Health To see recent Google Health activity in the server log: The log never contains tokens, health data, or locations. When reporting a problem, include the complete error and stack trace around the failing job. To stop syncing, select Disconnect Google ; your data stays. To delete the local copy, disconnect first, then select Delete local mirror and type DELETE. This removes only Google Health records and routes. ### Synchronization settings Most installations don't need to change these. Add them under mtl.google-health in the server configuration. | Setting | Default | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | history-start-date | 2010-01-01 | Oldest day to import | | recent-window | P7D | Days that are checked again for late changes | | recent-fast-window | PT24H | Range checked on every sync | | recent-full-interval | PT24H | How often the whole recent window is checked | | sync-interval | PT30M | Time between syncs | | cycle-deadline-margin | PT1M | Time kept free before the next sync | | history-budget-fraction | 0.5 | Share of sync time used for older history | | history-stream-quantum | PT1M | Time needed to start another page of history | | database-transaction-timeout | PT5M | Time limit for saving one batch | | work-failure-limit | 4 | Attempts before a failing range is skipped | | work-retry-max-delay | PT6H | Longest wait between retries | | max-chunk-rows / max-chunk-bytes | 100000 / 67108864 | Size limit per batch | See synchronization for how syncing works and which values are allowed.

title: Installation
text: # Installation - Host requirements - Install with Docker Compose - Install on a NAS

title: Install on a NAS
text: # Install on a NAS 1. Check the NAS against the host requirements : processor type, memory, free ports, and disk space. 2. Create a folder for MTL Explorer on a NAS share that is kept permanently, not a temporary or cache folder. Keep docker-compose.yml, .env, and data/ together in that folder. 3. Install with Docker Compose , using the NAS container manager or a terminal. 4. Open http://<nas-address>:18080/mtl/ from a browser on the same network. 5. Change the login . Set up HTTPS if you want to reach it from outside. 6. Test one import, one planned route, and a backup and restore . Make sure MTL Explorer can read your GPS folder and write to data/. If imports fail with "permission denied", check the folder permissions in your NAS settings. ## Updating Some NAS container managers keep their own copy of the Compose file. When you update , replace that copy with the new Compose file too; new images alone are not enough. Then recreate the containers in the container manager; a plain restart does not apply changed settings.

title: Install with Docker Compose
text: # Install with Docker Compose You need Docker with Compose. Check the host requirements first. 1. Create a folder for MTL Explorer and start it. On macOS, Linux, WSL, or Git Bash: On Windows PowerShell: The first start downloads the images and sets up the database. This can take several minutes. 2. Open http://localhost:18080/mtl/ and sign in with user mtl and password change-me. 3. Before other people or the internet can reach it, change the password . 4. Upload one supported GPS file and check that it appears on the map. Get started walks you through it. Everything MTL Explorer stores goes into the data/ folder next to docker-compose.yml. Keep this folder: it holds your database, maps, and routing data. ## If it does not start Check that all services are running and read their latest log lines: See troubleshooting for common problems.

title: Host requirements
text: # Host requirements MTL Explorer runs several services together: the app, a database, and route planning. It needs more memory than a small web app. - Docker with Compose. On Windows and macOS, install Docker Desktop. - A 64-bit Intel/AMD (linux/amd64) or ARM (linux/arm64) host. - At least 4 GB of memory; 6–8 GB is more comfortable. - Free ports 18080 (app) and 18083 (location search). Port 18081 is only needed for optional offline maps. - A stable internet connection for the online maps. Offline maps for the whole world need about 200 GB of free disk space. By default the services use about 2.5 GB of memory together. If you have many photos and videos or very long tracks, give the app more memory. See memory tuning . Use docker compose (with a space). The older docker-compose command is not supported.

title: Maintenance
text: # Maintenance - Back up and restore - Updates - Indexing and background work - Logs and retention

title: Back up and restore
text: # Back up and restore Your GPS files alone are not enough to recover everything. The database also holds your saved plans, corrections, review decisions, and health records. Back up: - the database and its user accounts (commands below) - your original GPS files, photos, and videos - docker-compose.yml, .env, and any override files - other folders you mounted yourself Store the backup privately on another disk or computer; it contains passwords and personal data. Note which image versions you were running. ## Create a consistent backup Run these commands in the folder with docker-compose.yml. Replace the example path with your backup location. MTL Explorer is stopped while the backup runs. Check that both commands succeeded and both files are not empty. roles.sql contains password hashes; keep it private. Without it, filters can stop working after a restore. Now copy docker-compose.yml, .env, override files, and your GPS, photo, and video folders. Copy the map and routing data too if you don't want to download it again. Don't add or change files while copying. Don't copy the data/postgis/ folder instead of making a dump; a copy of a running database may not restore. To check the dump, list its contents: Start MTL Explorer again when the backup is complete: ## Restore into a separate installation 1. Create a new installation directory. Restore configuration and source folders. Keep the same paths inside containers and use a fresh database directory. 2. Pin compatible images from the backup. Use separate host ports if the original instance is still running. 3. Bootstrap the new database with an administrator name absent from the role backup. For example, add this to compose.override.yml, merging any existing overrides: Keep the restored database username and password unchanged. The temporary administrator avoids conflicts when the original accounts are restored. Start only the database, leaving the app stopped: When the database is ready, restore the accounts first, then the data: Before starting the app, give the restored installation a new identity. This makes browsers discard cached tracks from before the restore, including when you restore to the same address: If you use Google Health, keep the same client secret in .env. With a new secret you must reconnect Google Health; your stored health data stays. Check the restored installation: login, number of tracks, a few tracks, saved plans, photo corrections, and review decisions. Download one original file. Wait for Settings → Processing to finish before you reload. Keep the old installation until you are sure the new one works. Going back to an older image does not undo data changes. To return to an older version, restore a backup made with that version.

title: Logs
text: # Logs Open Settings → Logs to see what the server and browsers reported. - Stored events lists errors and warnings from the server and from browsers. Filter by source, severity, topic, and time, then click Refresh . Open a row to see the full error. - Server file shows the latest lines of the server log. Browser problems also appear in Server file as short Client problem entries. Open the stored event for the full details. To turn off both viewers, set mtl.log-viewer-enabled=false. ## Retention Stored events are deleted after 30 days by default: If events pile up faster than they are deleted, increase cleanup-batch-size or shorten cleanup-interval. Set retention-enabled: false to keep all events. See diagnostic logging for the API and technical details.

title: Indexing and background work
text: # Indexing and background work Settings → Processing shows what MTL Explorer is working on: importing GPS files and photos, and calculations such as duplicates, activity types, energy, and exploration. Importing a file and finishing all its calculations can end at different times. ## Read the progress Complete · 100% means every file has a result. It does not mean every file was imported: some may have failed or been skipped. Open Technical details → Show failed files or Show skipped files to see which files and why. When files need attention, a card at the top shows N files need review . Click Review to check them. Fixing happens in Review , not in Processing; see Review . A Waiting task shows what it needs before it can continue. Select the linked task to inspect it. Automatic waits resume without your input. Open Details to see which tasks it depends on. In demos with synthetic health enabled, Google Health (beta) under Imports & sync shows Synthetic demo data and its progress in days. ## Rescan files MTL Explorer picks up new GPS files right away and rescans the GPS folder every 12 hours. Photos and videos are not watched: they are scanned when the server starts and every seven days. To pick up changes now, use Settings → Maintenance → Rescan GPS or Rescan Media . A rescan also retries files that failed before. It does not restore a database. Advanced settings: | Setting | Default | | --- | --- | | mtl.indexer.gps.live-watch-enabled | true | | mtl.indexer.gps.rescan-interval | PT12H | | mtl.indexer.media.live-watch-enabled | false | | mtl.indexer.media.rescan-interval | P7D | | mtl.indexer.gps.conversion-timeout | PT10M, time allowed to convert one non-GPX file | ## Keep your originals MTL Explorer never changes or deletes your original files. Keep them in place: they are needed to re-import tracks after an update. To reset the database, see Start with a fresh database . When the map shows a reload notice, open Settings → Data status or click Reload to see the latest results. See GPS processing for technical details.

title: Updates
text: # Updates Settings → Updates shows new releases, their release notes, and how to update the app and the services you run yourself. ## Update 1. Read the release notes for the new version. Some releases need extra steps. 2. Back up your installation. 3. Run docker compose version (with a space). If it fails, update Docker; the older docker-compose command is not supported. 4. Get the new Compose file. Downloading new images does not update it. Save the new file as docker-compose.new.yml next to your current one, or run: 5. Copy your own changes from docker-compose.yml into docker-compose.new.yml: folders, ports, and any memory limits you raised; set memswap_limit to the same value. Take everything else from the new file; .env stays as it is. Then rename the old file to docker-compose.old.yml and the new one to docker-compose.yml. If your NAS container manager keeps its own copy, paste the new file there. 6. In the folder with docker-compose.yml, check the file, download the new images, and restart the services: The first command prints nothing if the file is fine. If you use offline maps , add --profile local-maps to the last two commands. 7. Check that everything is running: 8. Open Settings → Processing and wait until it finishes. Then click Reload when the map asks. Keep your original GPS files in place. An update may re-read them once. ## Start with a fresh database Some release notes recommend a fresh database. MTL Explorer then imports your GPS and media files again. A fresh database deletes saved plans, manual edits, imported Health data, and the Google Health connection. Back up first. 1. Back up your installation. 2. In the folder with docker-compose.yml, stop MTL Explorer: 3. Rename the database folder. Keep it until you are sure you don't need to go back: 4. Continue with Update from step 3. MTL Explorer starts with an empty database. 5. If you use Google Health, connect your Google account again. Your settings in .env stay. MTL Explorer then imports your Health history again. 6. When Settings → Processing is finished, your tracks look right, and your Health history is back, delete data/postgis-old. ## Update check The update check is optional. If the server cannot reach the internet, the app works normally. To turn it off, add MTL_UPDATES_ENABLED=false to .env. To use your own release feed, set MTL_UPDATES_FEED_URL in .env. Then run docker compose up -d. See release updates for details. ## Pin exact versions To run a tested combination of images, set MTL_APP_IMAGE, MTL_BROUTER_IMAGE, MTL_LOCATION_SEARCH_IMAGE, and optional MTL_MAP_IMAGE in .env to the image digests listed in the release manifest. See component bundles . To build the images yourself from the source code, see container build .

title: Services
text: # Services MTL Explorer runs a few helper services next to the app. - Maps : online by default, offline maps optional. - Route planning : included and always on. - Place search : included and always on.

title: Place search
text: # Place search The map search finds towns, villages, and terrain features such as peaks, passes, ridges, and hills. It uses a GeoNames database that runs in its own location-search service. It does not find shops, addresses, or other points of interest.

title: Map services
text: # Map services By default, the base map loads from an online map service through your MTL Explorer server, so your browser doesn't contact that service for it. Other map parts, such as fonts, symbols, 3D terrain, some map styles, and trail overlays, load directly from their own services. ## Offline maps To host the base map yourself, enable the local-maps profile: 1. Add this line to .env: 2. Start with the profile: The first download is about 120–130 GB; keep about 200 GB free. It continues if interrupted and is saved in ./data/maps/. Keep this folder when you update; a new map image reuses the downloaded maps. Some map styles, 3D terrain, and trail overlays still load from the internet. Offline maps on the server are not the same as using the app offline on your phone; see mobile and offline use . For the simpler online setup, leave the local-maps profile off.

title: Route planning service
text: # Route planning service Route planning uses BRouter, which starts with MTL Explorer. Its routing data is saved in ./data/brouter-segments/. Keep this folder when you update. If route planning does not work, check the BRouter log:

title: Diagnose an installation
text: # Diagnose an installation First check that all services are running, then read the latest log lines: | Problem | What to check | | --- | --- | | App does not start | Is the database ready? Do the image and Compose file belong to the same version? Can the app read its folders? | | Files are not imported | Is the GPS folder mounted where you expect? Can the app read it? Is the format supported? Open Review for errors. | | Offline maps missing | Is the local-maps profile on? Has the download finished? Is there enough disk space? | | Route planning fails | Is routing data downloaded? Check the BRouter log. | | Place search finds nothing | Is the location-search service running? | | Google Health cannot connect | See Google Health setup . | | Browser shows old data | Open Settings → Data status , or reload when the app asks. | Fix the cause before restarting again and again. Keep your original files and backups. To recover data, see backup and restore .

title: Architecture
text: # Architecture Current system responsibilities and contracts. Future designs and dated investigations are maintained internally. Start with the system overview . - Database relation diagrams - GPS ingestion, processing, and quality - Energy, exploration, and segment calculations - Filtering and map coloring - Media indexing, correlation, and delivery - Source issues and account acknowledgements - Google Health authorization and synchronization - Map delivery , map interactions , and Garmin export - Planning and Replay - Browser caches and offline behavior - Processing status and dependencies - Diagnostic logging - Units and display conversion - Accepted decisions Build and test instructions are in Development .

title: Analysis contracts
text: # Analysis contracts - Energy and power estimates - Exploration Score - Segment analysis contract

title: Energy and power estimates
text: # Energy and power estimates ## Mechanical work and power EnergyService calculates external mechanical work from supported canonical intervals after activity classification. Models account for applicable climbing, drag, rolling/friction, and acceleration. Mechanical Wh and metabolic kcal are separate results; measured device-power series are not imported by this model. Moving average power divides work during stored moving intervals by their elapsed time. Normalized Power uses a trailing 30-second window and fourth-power weighting; Max 30 s Power is the highest trailing average. Segment summaries retain their separate full-density maximum-power contract. Statistics aggregates mechanical work and derived power metrics, not metabolic calories. Intensity Index is Normalized Power divided by the configured threshold; Training Load is its square times moving hours times 100. The configuration key is fitness/user/thresholdPowerWatts in config, with a 150 W fallback. This is an installation setting, not a measured personal threshold or a per-user account. See EnergyService for current calculations and configuration. ## Persistence and timing The durable energy worker locks each track and calculates from canonical points in one transaction. Points are loaded as read-only Hibernate entities; the existing point repository uses a native bulk query to write only the eight energy/power fields. The track repository writes only the mechanical, metabolic, and power summary fields. The loaded track remains an unchanged calculation input; worker diagnostics go to the server log. A failed chunk rolls back the track's complete calculation. The queue acknowledges only the generation it read, after the calculation transaction commits. Canonical-point changes queue photo correlation only when interpolation inputs change: parent, position, timestamp, ordering, altitude, interval qualification, cumulative distance, or elapsed time. Energy-only updates do not queue photos. The service logs load, calculation, and point-write phases before commit. The worker's Track energy transaction committed timer includes transaction flush and commit; batch timing also includes queue acknowledgments. ## Metabolic calories Track Overview shows estimated active calories and total calories alongside mechanical work. The weight dialog previews and saves both calculations. Calories describe the person; vehicle work is never converted into human calories. Active calories exclude standard resting expenditure. Total calories add rest for the same covered intervals. The conversion uses 1 MET = 3.5 ml O₂/(kg min) and 5 kcal/l O₂ (1.05 kcal/(kg h)). Recorded stops contribute rest only. Body weight, method, model version, coverage and totals are stored in gps_track. ## Activity models | Activity | Model for moving intervals | |---|---| | Walking, hiking | Minetti walking cost by grade, body weight and surface distance | | Running | Minetti running cost by grade, body weight and surface distance | | Bicycle | ACSM leg cycling equation applied to estimated mechanical power | | Mountain biking | Compendium general mountain biking: 8.5 MET | | Rowing | Compendium recreational rowing: 3.5 MET | | Kayaking | Compendium moderate kayaking: 5 MET | | Stand-up paddle | Compendium general stand-up paddling: 6.5 MET | | Skiing | Compendium general skiing: 7 MET | | Car | Compendium passenger: 1.3 MET; driver/passenger role is unknown | | Motorbiking | Compendium motorcycling: 2.8 MET | | Airplane, supersonic | Seated passenger proxy: 1.3 MET; no aircraft-energy contribution | ## Models and limits Minetti et al. (2002) provides net locomotion costs in J/(kg m). The published grade polynomials are evaluated only within −45% to +45%. Smoothed grade is preferred, with denoised elevation differences as fallback only over at least one metre of horizontal distance. A valid smoothed grade does not require endpoint elevations. Horizontal GPS distance is converted to distance along the slope. Downhill cost stays positive and increases again on steep descents. Walking assumes an economical pace on firm ground; it is not a backpack-load or technical-terrain model. Equipment mass is not substituted for body mass. No extra climbing term is added because the cost curve already includes grade. The ACSM cycling equation is VO₂ = 7 + 10.8 × watts / bodyWeightKg, in ml/(kg min). The resting term is subtracted once for active calories. See the equation used by Swain et al. (2004) . This is an outdoor approximation of a steady-state ergometer model, most applicable at moderate power. The unloaded-pedaling term supplies a light movement allowance while coasting; GPS cannot establish cadence or distinguish all pedaling from braking. The input is estimated external work, without a measured drivetrain correction. Wind, assistance and individual efficiency are unknown. Intervals whose mechanical energy was limited as implausible are omitted. Cycling also requires a finite accepted elevation change for each moving interval; absent elevation cannot be treated as flat. Other activities use the 2024 Compendium : cycling , water activities , winter activities and transportation . These are coarse population averages, not individualized measurements. Skiing does not identify lift rides; water activities do not identify drift; MTB does not resolve technical difficulty. The GUI states the assumption for each model. No heart-rate calibration or device calorie totals are mixed into these estimates. ## Coverage and recalculation Only supported, timed intervals with known moving/stopped state contribute. Missing grade and elevation for graded locomotion, invalid time, unknown motion, recording gaps, sparse sampling and unsupported gradients are omitted. Exact repeated observations with the same timestamp and no horizontal or vertical movement are harmless; untimed movement remains excluded. A partial estimate is the sum of covered intervals, never extrapolated to the full track. If none are covered, calories are unavailable, not zero. Missing timestamps can leave unquantifiable excluded time. New imports and activity changes use the existing energy queue and canonical points. Google Health exercise association queues energy for the first classification or a changed activity type. Repeated metadata, source attribution, and aliases that map to the same activity preserve calculated results and pending retry requests. The comparison locks the current track in the association transaction. Activity edits clear the previous totals and commit a durable queue request with the new activity. Failures remain queued for retry. Metadata saves apply editable fields to the locked current track, preserving every background result instead of merging a client copy. Source replacements preserve saved body weight without copying old calories. Weight changes save mechanical and metabolic totals together. The detail view reloads energy charts after completed changes, with HTTP cache revalidation. Changeset 082 requests a one-time full GPS reimport for upgrades from the previous release. Changeset 089 adds the metabolic columns and requests the existing energy worker once for ready imported tracks, including development databases where 082 already ran. It does not reset source files or delete tracks. Subsequent startups do not repeat either completed migration. See release upgrade instructions . Changeset 090 adds nullable coverage-explanation fields without a backfill. Saved body weight takes precedence over the configured default for recalculation and previews. Configured weights must be finite and within 35–180 kg; invalid values use 75 kg. Water-sport external work includes drag and acceleration, with altitude changes excluded. River descent is not credited against paddling work, and elevation noise cannot add ascent work. Water-sport calorie models remain the activity MET estimates listed above. Moving intervals with unavailable or limited mechanical work are excluded. Intervals whose estimated mechanical work exceeds gross metabolic energy are also excluded with an explicit reason. This is a physical consistency check, not a calibrated intensity or water-current model. Known zero speeds are preserved before any average-speed fallback. Model version 2026-09-30-v3 identifies this implementation. These are track totals; metabolic time-series charts and metabolic segment/statistics aggregation are not part of this version. See the user guide for the controls.

title: Exploration Score
text: # Exploration Score Exploration Score estimates the fraction of a track's supported path that is new relative to earlier eligible archive tracks. It is a value from 0 to 1, displayed as a percentage. It describes the imported archive, not all places the person has visited. ## Calculation ExplorationScoreQueryRepository owns the PostGIS query; ExplorationScoreAtomicWorker stores the result. 1. Read the configured SIMPLIFIED_SHAPE precision's observed_path, which omits connecting edges across recording gaps. 2. Transform that path to EPSG:3857 and split its line segments to at most corridor-width-m projected meters. 3. Prepare each target segment's search bounds once. Filter eligible earlier track IDs using their maintained source bounds, then retrieve each selected shape by ID and project its observed path once. Reuse these candidates for the original geometry bounding-box and ST_DWithin checks. Combining the segment bounds keeps the target prefilter conservative at the antimeridian. 4. Sum unmatched segment lengths and divide by total supported length. Java clamps the ratio to [0, 1] and rounds it to three decimal places. Prior tracks must have an earlier start_date, successful load, and UNIQUE duplicate status. Both targets and prior tracks exclude review_excluded and timing_unreliable recordings. Duplicate classification and GPS indexing must settle before the job starts. The query uses EPSG:3857 distances, not ground-distance geodesics. Projection distortion, simplified geometry, the corridor threshold, and whole-segment classification limit accuracy. A segment is considered known when any part comes within the corridor; this is not an exact polygon difference. Materialized SQL intermediate results avoid repeating archive searches and coordinate transforms per segment. They can spill to temporary disk under the existing database memory settings. The calculation keeps no Java archive cache and does not skip scheduled targets based on duplicate status. Large candidate sets still need runtime memory and disk capacity. The source bounds are maintained during ingest. A named 0.001-degree prefilter margin conservatively covers shape snapping to a 0.00001-degree grid, six-decimal bound rounding, and spatial bounding-box precision. It does not widen the scoring corridor: the original geometry predicates still determine coverage. Two partial indexes support candidate selection: a date/bounds index for eligible prior tracks, with ID included, and an ID index for the 10 m SIMPLIFIED_SHAPE variant. Bounds are index keys so rejected candidates avoid heap visibility checks. Matching candidates can still require heap reads after updates. The default query uses fixed type and precision literals for generic prepared plans; other precisions use bound parameters and the general ID index. The lateral lookup's OFFSET 0 keeps geometry retrieval per selected ID. Migration 093 replaces the earlier exploration indexes: retaining that partial spatial index can cause repeated area scans inside the per-ID lookup. The existing general geometry index remains available. Regression tests cover the actual migration and JDBC auto/custom/generic plans. Dense late tracks can still favor the earlier spatial strategy; archive benchmarks should include them. ## Configuration The shipped application configuration sets: The class fallback for worker-threads is 3, but the shipped configuration uses 1 to avoid overlapping large geometry queries. Supported stored shape precisions are 1, 10, 100, and 1000 meters. Choose a precision that is actually generated; zero is not a raw-data mode for this query. A full batch immediately continues through the scheduler's loop. The normal delay applies after pending work drains or a guard stops processing. Throughput depends on geometry size, archive density, and database resources; batch size is not a runtime bound. ## State and invalidation | Status | Meaning | | --- | --- | | NOT_SCHEDULED | Not eligible or no usable geometry/date for calculation. | | SCHEDULED | Awaiting calculation. | | IN_PROGRESS | Accepted when reading pending work; current workers keep the pending state until completion. | | CALCULATED | A stored score is available. | | NEEDS_RECALCULATION | Invalidated result or a calculation to retry. | ExplorationScoreJob checks for newly scheduled historical imports and invalidates later overlapping calculated tracks through a repository update. Source-review changes also invalidate affected nearby scores and release duplicate relationships. Unrelated scores remain available. The job compares corridor and precision settings with its stored config snapshot. A change resets calculated scores for recalculation. Worker count, batch size, and schedule do not change the score definition. Each worker uses its own transaction and writes only exploration status, score, and calculation date through targeted repository updates. The loaded track remains unchanged. The write happens after the query, allowing other jobs to commit during calculation. Missing eligible geometry clears the score and sets NOT_SCHEDULED; calculation failures are logged and marked NEEDS_RECALCULATION. Only score, status, and calculation time are stored on gps_track. Multiplying the score by a full-track distance is an estimate of new ground, not the exact projected novel_m used internally by this query.

title: Segment analysis contract
text: # Segment analysis contract Crossing discovery issues one opaque reference for each consecutive ordered zone/visit pair. The signed descriptor contains the track, ordered zone visits, canonical fractional positions, and zone/source revisions. Times, coordinates and measurements are reconstructed from the revision-checked canonical source using the discovery rules. Stored point IDs do not define the interval. Import, discovery, and interval clipping share RecordingContinuity geometry rules. Nearby duplicate timestamps retain geometry support without inventing interior crossing timestamps. Explicit recording gaps and unsupported stored intervals split discovery. Consecutive known timestamps also expose gaps across untimed observations. Supported endpoint elapsed time remains available across a path gap when the clock is coherent; complete distance and average speed remain unavailable. Clock resets invalidate elapsed time even when the final endpoint difference is positive. The requested radius is the inner qualification circle. Zone departure uses an exit radius of radius + max(2 m, 20% × radius); closest approach still selects the visit's point. A crossing within any confirmed nonzero stationary span, including identical coordinates, produces AMBIGUOUS_DWELL timing for both adjacent attempts. Distance retains canonical observed geometry; no stationary coordinates are rewritten. Discovery requires actual visits to every requested zone. Per-zone counts are exact within the filtered population before the complete-route intersection. Full timing and metric processing is limited to the candidate intersection. Each track's crossings, revision and attempt summaries are calculated in a separate read-only persistence context, which closes before the next track loads. Only compact results remain in the response. Other candidates use geometry and continuity projections one track at a time for exact per-zone qualification. Source memory therefore depends on the largest individual track; response memory still grows with the number of visits. Preliminary map counts are candidates. Candidate SQL uses canonical recorded paths, densified along the same wrapped lon/lat curve with a 0.25 m allowance; isolated fixes are retained without connecting recording gaps. Stop notes use canonical stationary spans clipped by position and time. Total stopped time includes short pauses; break count and longest break use the one-minute visible-break threshold. Ambiguous marker timing or incomplete motion/path coverage makes these observed lower bounds. SegmentAttemptResolver owns reference validation. References are signed server descriptors scoped to the authenticated user and expire after 30 minutes. Their signing key is derived separately from the persisted login key, so cache eviction and application restarts do not invalidate unchanged attempts. Expired, invalid, deleted, or changed sources return HTTP 410; another owner receives HTTP 404. The comparison offers Refresh results . No persistent attempt entity is needed. The canonical revision includes point metrics and relevant events, covering changes that do not increment the parent track version. Every core, health, and comparison request revalidates it. Core results are cached for ten minutes with a 250,000-source-point weight limit. Optional health responses are uncached and use one repeatable-read database snapshot. Browser caches are disabled for these endpoints. ## Calculation ownership | Server responsibility | Rule | | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Identity and clipping | All services use the same resolved attempt. Exact analysis endpoints retain their measurements; virtual speed/slope interpolate the full-track physics window samples, while raw estimated power belongs to the interval's ending fix. Display windows are computed over the full track before clipping. | | Distance, elapsed time, average speed | Use discovery's authoritative values with separate availability. Cumulative distance becomes unavailable after unsupported path coverage. Supported geometry progress ends at the authoritative distance; only discrepancies up to 1 cm are reconciled. Larger discrepancies log a diagnostic and make distance, speed and distance progress unavailable with DISTANCE_MISMATCH; elapsed time and independent metrics remain inspectable. Validation runs before discovery summaries are published. Recording breaks remain explicit. | | Energy | Sum canonical interval work, prorated at fractional boundaries. Never subtract an invented whole-track baseline. An unsupported interval makes total energy unavailable; a supported initial prefix can remain visible as incomplete coverage. | | Ascent/descent and maximum power | Calculate before series reduction. Unsupported cumulative elevation boundaries produce unavailable totals. Maximum power covers available endpoint and interior estimates. | | Ordinary HR | Integrate raw BPM over canonical recorded support, including detected stops. Keep surrounding samples for integration, restrict recorded chart samples before bucketing, and preserve the existing BPM sample-gap limit. A sample with unavailable map distance can still appear on the time axis. | | Cardiac cost | Use the same exact interval but retain the existing covered moving-time and minimum-work rules. Coasting counts; detected stops do not. | | Consolidation | Arithmetic means with separate valid counts for elapsed time, distance, and visit speed. Incomplete path coverage and distance mismatches are excluded from performance means and default trends; individual endpoint elapsed times remain inspectable. Total visits and valid metric counts remain separate. HR uses covered-time weighting. | | Comparison | Finish difference and equal-distance difference are separate results. Equal-distance interpolation has no extrapolation and preserves arrival and the limit after a stop. It requires the same ordered zone pair and zone revision. | | Ghosts | For each reference distance, the attempt's distance at the reference's arrival time and the resulting lead. Samples cover the reference's timed geometry plus the attempt's own sample times. A reference stop adds a departure sample; an attempt past its end is FINISHED at its final distance; recording breaks are UNAVAILABLE. | The client selects, requests, formats, and renders generated API values. It may interpolate map display positions within supported server geometry; it does not rebuild analytical totals, health averages, or time-gap curves. One selection owner handles reference validity, request generations, cancellation, and per-track retries. Core and health use independent pools of at most four requests each. Core chart series share ChartSeriesMetrics and ChartBucketBuilder with track details: windowed speed/power, averaged elevation/slope, and last cumulative energy per bucket. Walking/hiking uses a 60-second display window; other activities use 30 seconds. The x request selects time or distance bucketing. Comparison Graph settings starts collapsed and reuses the saved track-detail Points (3–3,000) and Height (100–640 px) preferences. Height resizes all comparison graphs without requesting data. Counts are soft limits: exact endpoints, stops, gaps and null transitions take priority. Instantaneous maximum power remains a separate full-density summary. Full geometry and comparison breakpoints are retained. Large canonical tracks therefore still have a source-size-dependent response and calculation cost; chart reduction never changes the summaries. ## API and verification Discovery uses includeHealth=false for independent core loading. Existing callers retain the default inline HR behavior. The generated SegmentAnalysisControllerApi exposes core, health, comparison, and per-track table-HR requests. DTO units are explicit; unavailable optional fields may be absent or null, and display conversion preserves both as unavailable. The schema is exported from the running server at /mtl/v3/api-docs, retaining http://localhost:8080/mtl as its server URL. Maven generates the TypeScript package in the development container; there is no new generator workaround. Current segment tests cover exact boundaries, references, health support, and comparisons. Use the testing workflow for new verification. Changed derived geometry and continuity metadata require reimporting existing tracks, or recreating the database. No legacy-data backfill is provided. Calculation version changes invalidate previous attempt references.

title: Browser caching and offline behavior
text: # Browser caching and offline behavior The PWA shell, track cache, map archive cache, media responses, and browser preferences have separate lifecycles. Cached display data is not an alternative owner of server calculations. Server/client freshness domains compare revision tokens after ingest and job changes. New requests must not let older results restore a superseded selection. Source changes invalidate exact segment attempt references and relevant derived results. A cache-first archive can show previously available tracks while refreshing. Uncached content and server-backed calculations still need connectivity. Hosted terrain, overlays, and account services can have independent network requirements. Service-worker updates wait for an explicit reload. Session cleanup can remove browser data; credentials-only sign-out has a narrower scope. Source acknowledgements belong to the server account and survive either sign-out flow. They do not dismiss processing, offline, service, or stale-map indicators. Freshness detection and reload remain available without a snooze or dismiss handler. See PWA configuration , track cache , and user limits .

title: Database relations
text: # Database relations MTL Explorer uses PostgreSQL with PostGIS. These diagrams cover all 38 foreign keys and list all 42 application tables in the schema through Liquibase change 111. Table names without a schema prefix belong to public. Only keys and selected fields are shown; the Liquibase changelog defines the complete schema. ## Reading the diagrams Every line represents an enforced foreign key; its label names the child column. PK means primary key and FK means foreign key. UK marks a unique key; multiple fields marked UK in a table form one composite key. A circle means zero is allowed, a bar means one, and a crow's foot means many. Cardinalities describe what the database allows. Solid lines use a foreign key as part of the child's primary key; dashed lines use a separate key. Nullable fields are noted where they affect a relationship. ## Tracks and derived data Tracks, derived geometry, events, and recalculation relations Mermaid source . An indexed file can produce several tracks. duplicate_of and source_parent_track_id reference other rows in gps_track. Track geometry, point calculations, and events are stored separately. Saved plans also use gps_track; track_source distinguishes their origin. See GPS processing . The database owns gps_track.version. Metadata writes increment it, and statement triggers on gps_track_data also revise each affected parent once per statement when stored geometry variants are inserted, updated, moved or deleted. An import inserts each geometry variant separately, so it advances the version several times. Version-only updates do not create metadata audit snapshots ( change 112 ). Individual point writes do not invoke these triggers. This lets the client reuse unchanged track caches while refreshing metadata and all geometry precisions for revised tracks. See change 111 . Cache reuse assumes one database history. The restore procedure rotates the installation identity before startup, including restores to the same address. Browsers also discard the cache when a freshness revision decreases. An unannounced restore whose counters have already caught up cannot be detected from IDs and versions alone; rotating the identity is required. ## Source review and acknowledgements Source diagnosis, use decisions, issues, and account acknowledgements Mermaid source . Source reviews, use decisions, and issues refer to the indexed file. An issue can have one acknowledgement per account_key; that key is an authenticated account name, with no database account table. See source issues . ## Media and track correlation Media files, corrections, locations, track correlation, and work queues Mermaid source . Media and tracks are related through media_track_correlation. Its composite unique key permits one candidate per media/track pair. A partial unique index allows at most one selected candidate per media file. Corrections, resolved locations, calculation state, and work queues have at most one row per owning media file or track. See media correlation . ## Google Health records and route ownership Google Health connection, mirrored records, sources, and imported route links Mermaid source . The google_health schema isolates connection state and imported Health records. connection.id is constrained to 1. Routes can refer to normal indexed files and GPS tracks; deletion of those public rows sets the Health references to null. Deleting a connection cascades to sync_state, data_source, data_point, and heart_rate_sample. The route_ownership connection reference has no cascade. Heart-rate identity uniqueness uses partial indexes: named records use (connection_id, identity_key) and unnamed records use (connection_id, sample_time, identity_key). These are omitted from the field key markers. See Health synchronization . ## Google Health synchronization work Google Health recent passes, retries, historical work, child traversal, and audit Mermaid source . history_child.parent_id is the only foreign key in this group. Account-scoped tables share the Google account ID by application convention. Their account_id columns have no foreign key to connection.google_user_id or sync_control. history_audit.work_id and traversal_ids retain logical work/traversal references without foreign keys. ## Client login and request logs Client login references used by request and browser environment logs Mermaid source . Both log tables reference the unique client_login_ref, rather than the login row's id. A log may have no login reference. The login's last-log IDs are application links without foreign keys. system_log.client_login_ref also has no foreign key. Its nullable stack_fingerprint has a non-unique index and is calculated from the full captured stack when a client report is submitted. Existing rows retain null. See diagnostic logging . ## Tables without foreign keys These nine public tables complete the application table inventory. | Table | Purpose | | --- | --- | | config | Stored settings, keyed by id | | filter_config | Filter definitions, keyed by id | | data_freshness | Domain revisions, keyed by domain_key | | system_log | Server and client diagnostics, keyed by id | | indexed_file_audit | Indexed-file change snapshots | | gps_track_audit | Track change snapshots | | media_file_audit | Media change snapshots | | config_audit | Setting change snapshots | | filter_config_audit | Filter change snapshots | Audit tables retain copied IDs and values without primary or foreign keys. They can retain history after deletion of the source row. ## Views and infrastructure gps_track_v joins tracks, indexed-file metadata, and derived geometry. media_file_v joins media and indexed-file metadata. These are query views, with no independent primary or foreign keys. Liquibase's databasechangelog and databasechangeloglock, PostGIS's spatial_ref_sys, and the PostGIS metadata views are excluded from the application table count. Diagram editing and rendering are described in the asset notes . ## Read-only database access Dynamic SQL uses the separate mtluserreadonly pool. New databases create the role without a password. After Liquibase completes, startup applies MTL_DB_READONLY_PASSWORD before opening that pool. An unset or blank value uses the configured primary database password. PostgreSQL quotes both the role and credential; the credential is excluded from startup diagnostics. Existing databases use the same startup path. The table and relation diagrams are unchanged.

title: Accepted architecture decisions
text: # Accepted architecture decisions These decisions describe current ownership. Detailed contracts are linked below. | Decision | Reason and current reference | | --- | --- | | Domain calculations run on the server | Shared canonical inputs and results; segment contract | | OpenAPI owns API types | Server export and generated client; API workflow | | Canonical metric units, converted presentation | Domain meaning stays server-owned; unit contract | | Source observations and processed geometry stay distinct | Preserve evidence and explicit support; GPS pipeline | | Display simplification does not own totals | Maps and reduced charts consume canonical results | | User corrections preserve media source evidence | Separate precedence and correlation; media contract | | Google Health uses installation-owned authorization | Local mirror and identity control; OAuth contract | Pending designs belong in internal proposals. After implementation, update the current contract and record the accepted decision here. Split this index into topic records when the number warrants it.

title: Diagnostic logging
text: # Diagnostic logging MTL Explorer stores client diagnostics and existing server operation events in system_log. Source, severity, topics, stack trace, structured JSON context, build ID, and login reference are nullable. Older rows retain their original values and unspecified classifications. The additive Liquibase change does not backfill or rewrite them; the existing timestamp type, creation-date behavior, and indexes remain. Use the shared singleton or its logSanitizedError / warnSanitized delegates: Metadata accepts stackTrace?: string | null. Omission extracts the original error stack; null suppresses extraction; a string supplies the trace. Sanitization retains frames and line breaks, including minified and Axios frames. The console receives the resolved record. The logger works before stores, router, or mounting. Vue, window, and promise rejection handlers share it and register browser listeners once. Optional startup diagnostics add no browser reporting listeners. Console redaction remains local. Normal startup and sign-in transitions remain informational and are not queued as problems. Startup warnings and errors take the original error and structured context as separate arguments. Context-only warnings have no exception type, description, or stack. See frontend error-handling rules . Startup warnings and errors report independently of the startupDiag toggle; the toggle controls verbose informational output. Map rendering and graphics-context failures, navigation errors, and selected media, routing, analysis, review, health, and administration failures use the same service. Cancellation, stale requests, normal teardown, speculative prefetch, and browser capability fallbacks stay local. Health and source-review reporting uses the original transport error before private response details are read for the UI. After local console logging, the client immediately starts persistence in a separate IndexedDB database through Dexie. Capture never uploads. Records carry a stable UUID, original occurrence time, build, and original login reference; credentials are never stored in the queue. Pending identical records within 60 seconds of their last occurrence consolidate into one record with an occurrence count and first/last times. Every occurrence is still logged to the console. Once an upload is attempted, its payload is immutable; later repetitions form another record so a retry always carries the same ID and content. Insertion and housekeeping share a transaction. Keep the newest 250 records, including sent and rejected records, and at most 4 MiB of serialized diagnostic payloads. Older unsent records can be evicted. Pending captures in memory have the same bounds while persistence is running. Oversized diagnostics retain a bounded rejected record locally; their full resolved record remains in the console. There is no legacy-data backfill. An independent sender checks every second and wakes on startup, login, connectivity changes, and return to the visible app. It sends retained pending records in insertion order, one request at a time, at most 25 per run. An IndexedDB lease coordinates tabs and expires after an abandoned sender. An idle check uses the pending-status index without loading retained payloads or writing delivery state. The rolling budget is 100 upload attempts per 60 seconds, persisted across reloads and shared between tabs for the same backend. Failed attempts count; exceeding the budget defers records without discarding them. Network, timeout, and server failures leave records pending and pause the queue with increasing retry delays, capped at 60 seconds. HTTP 429 honors Retry-After. HTTP 401 pauses until the login reference changes. Permanent invalid requests, including HTTP 403 for an invalid historical login reference, become rejected and do not block later reports. Successful server acknowledgment sets sent. The sender uses current credentials, a five-second request timeout, and a generated API configuration without auth redirects or reporting interceptors. Delivery failures never report themselves. Reports captured with an account remain scoped to that account and backend. Account comparisons follow the case-insensitive login rules. Pre-login diagnostics can be delivered after login and bind to that account on first attempt. Credentials-only logout retains the queue; forget-everything logout stops delivery and clears persistent and memory records, including other tabs. If IndexedDB opening or writing fails, the bounded memory queue continues delivery for that page session. It cannot survive reload; the persistent database is retried on the next startup. Browser storage can also be cleared or evicted. Page timers cannot deliver while the app is closed; reopening resumes the stored queue. POST /mtl/api/logs/client requires the existing authenticated API rule and returns 204 after insertion. Its explicit DTO requires nonblank message and build ID, accepts optional WARN/ERROR severity and nullable stack, and excludes entity ID, date, source, and login reference. The controller assigns CLIENT, the server storage time (createDate), and the validated current JWT login reference. Client occurredAt remains the original event time; repeated reports also carry lastOccurredAt and occurrenceCount. The optional original login reference is checked against the currently authenticated account. A unique client event ID makes retries idempotent, including concurrent retries. New fields are nullable for existing rows and callers. Invalid or oversized input is rejected; stacks are never truncated to fit. On client submission the server computes a nullable, indexed stackFingerprint using SHA-256 over the sanitized captured stack. It removes leading exception header/message lines, normalizes line endings and surrounding line whitespace, and keeps every remaining nonblank line in order, including all frames and their file, line, and column locations. V8 at ... and Firefox/Safari function@... frame starts are recognized. Missing or unrecognized stacks have no fingerprint. Message, detail, context, build, severity, and login references are excluded. The log list and detail APIs expose the fingerprint; reports remain separate and existing retry/counting behavior is unchanged. Browser formatting and changed bundle locations can produce different fingerprints. Existing rows are not backfilled. Source identifies the reporting side. A browser reporting an HTTP failure still produces a CLIENT event; this does not establish the failure's root cause. Limits: 128 KiB request, 4,096 message characters, 16,384 detail characters, 65,536 stack characters, 8 KiB context, 255 characters per topic, and 128 build characters. Safe context is limited to error type/code, HTTP method/status, route name, Vue information, source/line/column, browser/PWA mode, package version, component, and operation. Do not supply tokens, cookies, passwords, URL queries, private IDs, request/response bodies, health/location data, or raw application state. The client reporting service and ingestion controller redact URL credentials and absolute or relative URL queries while retaining stack line and column locations. Server writers use the existing service and independent insert transactions. Known classifications and emitting build identity are populated. Exception stacks have their own field. Best-effort server writers catch metadata, save, and commit failures; ingestion returns 503 on persistence failure and uses ordinary server logging. Each accepted client report also writes one bounded, single-line Client problem summary at INFO to the server file log. It contains the stored log ID, client severity, topics, a short sanitized message, exception type, and exception description. The client supplies the type in context.errorType and the description in detail (normally the original exception message). The file summary uses only their first line, limited to 64 and 256 characters respectively; absent values are unspecified. Full stacks, detail, and context remain in the database; the client severity does not set the server file-log level. See stored log administration . ## Client login reference Each successful login creates a ClientLoginRef and a signed JWT. The reference identifies that login in application logs and optional analytics. It cannot authenticate a request on its own; the valid JWT is the credential. After validating the JWT, the server checks the login's active state and expiry. Signing out revokes that login, so its JWT no longer grants access. | Contract | Name | | --- | --- | | Java and TypeScript field | clientLoginRef | | JWT claim, database column, and application log field | client_login_ref | The login record is stored in web_client_login; request and browser environment logs link to it by client_login_ref. See database relations . ## Stored event API GET /mtl/api/admin/system-logs and GET /mtl/api/admin/system-logs/{id} require authentication. List pages default to 50 rows, with a maximum of 200, ordered newest first with ID as the date tie-breaker. Event time uses the client's original occurrence time when present, falling back to server creation time. Null classifications appear as Unspecified . Stored content is rendered as text. Retention deletes one bounded batch per scheduled run, based on the server creation date. Cleanup failures use ordinary server logging. A schema rollout preserves existing rows and leaves new fields null.

title: Filter Configuration And Map Coloring
text: # Filter Configuration And Map Coloring This document describes how track filters are configured, persisted, exposed to the UI, and used for map coloring and legends. The important distinction is: - A filter decides which tracks are returned. - A filter can optionally assign each returned track to a group. - Metadata on the filter tells the UI how to organize the filter, sort groups, label groups, and choose colors. ## 1. Filter Storage Filters are stored in filter_config. Core identity and execution fields: | Column | Description | |---|---| | filter_domain | Domain the filter applies to. Currently GPS_TRACK. | | filter_name | Stable unique filter key within the domain. | | filter_type | Execution type. Currently SQL. | | filter_category | SYSTEM or USER. | | expression | SQL template used to resolve matching track IDs and optional groups. | | display_name | Human-facing filter name. | | description | Human-facing explanation and use case. | | display_order | Ordering within filter lists. The frontend also uses the lowest order in a group to order selector groups. | UI and coloring metadata: | Column | Description | |---|---| | filter_group | UI section for the filter selector, for example Date & Time, Performance, or People. | | group_semantics | What the returned group values mean. | | coloring_strategy | How colors should be assigned to groups. | | legend_sort_strategy | How the map and preview legends should be ordered. | | preferred_palette | Optional default palette key used when the user has not chosen a palette yet. | | group_label_template | Optional display template for raw group values. | | ui_metadata | Optional JSON metadata for UI hints, formatting, and optional params. | The audit table filter_config_audit mirrors these fields. The audit trigger must be updated whenever filter metadata columns are added. ## 2. Typed Metadata Values The database stores metadata as text columns, but Java models fixed metadata sets as enums with @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING). Source of truth: FilterConfigEntity ### GROUP_SEMANTICS | Value | Meaning | |---|---| | CATEGORICAL | Unordered names such as activity type, quality status, or person. | | DATE_BUCKET | Date-like buckets such as year or calendar day. | | ORDINAL | Ordered labels with a fixed known sequence, such as quarters or weekdays. | | NUMERIC_BUCKET | Numeric buckets, usually percentile-style values. | ### COLORING_STRATEGY | Value | Meaning | |---|---| | CATEGORICAL | Assign distinct colors per group. Encounter order should not matter after legend sorting. | | SEQUENTIAL_GRADIENT | Map ordered numeric group values onto a continuous palette. | ### LEGEND_SORT_STRATEGY | Value | Meaning | |---|---| | LABEL_ASC | Sort labels alphabetically, with numeric-aware comparison. | | NUMERIC_ASC | Sort numeric bucket values from low to high. | | COUNT_DESC | Sort groups by matching track count, largest first. | These dimensions are intentionally separate. For example, an ordered weekday filter has group_semantics = ORDINAL but still uses categorical colors. A speed gradient filter has group_semantics = NUMERIC_BUCKET and coloring_strategy = SEQUENTIAL_GRADIENT. ## 3. SQL Filter Contract A SQL filter returns at least: Grouped/coloring filters also return: The raw grp value is the stable group key used by the map layer and by group visibility toggles. The UI can display a friendlier label using metadata, but the raw key should remain stable. Most GPS track filters include the standard base filter: This keeps normal date, geo area, successful-load, duplicate, and planned-track constraints consistent across filters. ## 4. Filter Groups Current top-level UI groups are: | Group | Display-order range | Typical filters | |---|---:|---| | Core | 1000-1999 | Standard base filter. | | Activity | 2000-2999 | Activity type and motorized/non-motorized filters. | | Date & Time | 3000-3999 | Year, day, quarter, weekday, time of day. | | People | 4000-4999 | Personal YAML-defined companion filters. | | Performance | 5000-5999 | Average speed, distance, elevation gain, energy gradients. | | Quality | 6000-6999; Needs review uses 5990 | Needs review, suspicious, duplicate, and error filters. | | User | 9000-9899 | User-defined filters without a more specific group. | | Other | 9900+ | Fallback for uncategorized filters. | The frontend orders selector groups by the lowest display_order inside each group, then uses a small known-group fallback order only for ties or missing orders. This keeps the database metadata as the primary source of ordering truth while still giving unknown group names stable behavior. ## 5. Presentation Defaults preferred_palette describes the recommended first palette for a filter. Legend order is a client-side choice. The frontend stores user overrides in the client filter configuration, so changing legend order or palette does not mutate the system filter definition. An explicit No coloring choice stores palette.noColoring = true and survives reloads, paused drafts, and view changes. An unset palette can still receive the view's preferred default. Older saved empty choices with the No coloring label are migrated to the explicit choice. Reset clears the choice; Undo restores it. Changing views resets a custom category order to the new view's default. The view picker discloses this reset before applying the change. If legend_sort_strategy is missing, the frontend preserves the first-seen group order returned by the SQL query. Filters that need a specific default order should make that order explicit in SQL. Numeric ordering is only used when NUMERIC_ASC is selected by the user. The frontend uses preferred_palette when a filter is selected and no palette is active yet. It also replaces an obviously incompatible palette when switching between categorical and gradient filters: - gradient filter with categorical palette: switch to the filter's preferred gradient palette - categorical filter with gradient palette: switch to the filter's preferred categorical palette - categorical filter with an existing categorical palette: keep the user's current choice Current categorical defaults use existing palette keys: | Filter shape | Preferred palette | |---|---| | naturally small groups, such as quarters, motorized/non-motorized, quality filters | 005_COLORS | | weekday, time-of-day, activity, people, and general user filters | 008_COLORS | | standard base filter without groups | none | ui_metadata.optionalParams lists params that may be left blank even when they are rendered as editable fields, for example DATE_TIME_FROM, DATE_TIME_TO, or gradient min/max range params. ## 6. Gradient Filters Gradient filters are designed for ordered numeric buckets. Current gradient filters: | Filter | Metric | Unit | Params | |---|---|---|---| | TracksByAverageSpeedGradient | Average moving speed | km/h | AVG_SPEED_MIN_KMH, AVG_SPEED_MAX_KMH | | TracksByDistanceGradient | Track distance | km | DISTANCE_MIN_KM, DISTANCE_MAX_KM | | TracksByElevationGainGradient | Elevation gain | m | ELEVATION_GAIN_MIN_M, ELEVATION_GAIN_MAX_M | | TracksByEnergyGradient | Estimated net mechanical energy | kWh | ENERGY_MIN_KWH, ENERGY_MAX_KWH | These names and units are also exposed by the current filter API. The client uses filterParamUnits.ts to convert display input back to the metadata unit. The proposed public renames to meters and watt-hours have not been implemented; see the measurement-system status . Each gradient filter assigns the current result set to bucket values 0 to 99. The bucket is based on sorted rank within the filtered result set, not on an absolute metric threshold. This keeps the full color range useful for the visible tracks. For small result sets, the SQL scales rank positions across the full 0-99 range. With two tracks, the lower track gets bucket 0 and the higher track gets bucket 99. With one track, the bucket is 0. Recommended metadata for gradient filters: | Field | Value | |---|---| | group_semantics | NUMERIC_BUCKET | | coloring_strategy | SEQUENTIAL_GRADIENT | | preferred_palette | A GRADIENT_100_* palette, usually GRADIENT_100_VIRIDIS. | | group_label_template | A metric-specific label such as Avg speed percentile {bucket}. | The frontend maps bucket values to palette indices. A 100-color palette maps bucket 0 to the first color and bucket 99 to the last color. Shorter palettes are scaled proportionally. ## 7. Group Labels The raw group key should remain compact and stable. Display labels are derived in the UI. For numeric buckets, group_label_template supports: | Placeholder | Meaning | |---|---| | {bucket} | Zero-padded bucket based on the configured bucket count. For 100 buckets this is 00 to 99. | | {bucketNumber} | Raw numeric bucket without padding. | Example: This keeps legends readable while preserving numeric sorting. ## 8. YAML-Defined Filters Filters can also be supplied through application YAML under: Example metadata: The YAML properties bind directly to FilterConfigEntity, so enum values must match the Java enum names exactly. The initializer only creates YAML filters that do not already exist in the database. Editing YAML does not update an existing row. Do not add a historical backfill unless explicitly requested; follow backend migration policy and document when recreation is required. ## 9. OpenAPI And Frontend Types FilterConfigEntity is exposed through the OpenAPI schema. Because the metadata fields are Java enums, the generated TypeScript client exposes matching enum types. Frontend code should use the generated enum constants instead of duplicating raw strings. This keeps UI behavior aligned with the server contract. Relevant frontend behavior: - the filter selector groups filters by filter_group - the map legend and preview legend sort by the user override, otherwise preserve the first-seen group order returned by SQL - gradient filters use coloring_strategy = SEQUENTIAL_GRADIENT - display labels use group_label_template - gradient help text is based on ui_metadata ## 10. Key Source Files | File | Role | |---|---| | mtl-server/src/main/java/.../db/entity/config/FilterConfigEntity.java | JPA entity and metadata enums. | | mtl-server/src/main/java/.../logic/grouping/sql/custom/FilterConfigInitializer.java | Creates YAML-defined filters if missing. | | mtl-server/src/main/resources/db/changelog/changes/047.xml | Metadata columns, audit trigger update, backfills, gradient SQL updates. | | application.yml | User-defined filter configuration; see the examples above. | | mtl-client/src/utils/filterMetadata.ts | Frontend metadata interpretation, label formatting, legend sorting, gradient color mapping. | | mtl-client/src/components/filter/CustomFilter.vue | Filter selector, preview legend, palette guidance. | | mtl-client/src/components/map/Map2DRenderer.vue | Main map rendering. | | mtl-client/src/components/filter/FilterOverview.vue | Current filter view, criteria, categories, and review entry points. | | mtl-client/src/components/map/ColorPaletteLegend.vue | Map legend and visibility controls. |

title: Garmin export flow
text: # Garmin export flow MTL Explorer runs two community helpers from GarminExporter.
