An activity-type filter can yield a range spanning years. ## Related and unrelated media - All media is the default. It includes linked and unlinked photos and videos inside the interval. - Track related adds a requirement that the selected media correlation links to a matching track. The time interval remains the same. Both choices use the media’s own capture time: EXIF GPS time first, otherwise EXIF camera time with any saved camera correction. A track link cannot bring older, newer or undated media into the interval. File creation and import dates are not substitutes. Media without a usable capture date is excluded. ## Consistent views The main map, Overview media count, Trends chart/table and period mosaic use the same selection. The map additionally requires a location inside the loaded viewport, so its visible marker count can be smaller than the statistics count. Activity and media charts share aligned periods, with zero values where a series has no items. Choose All media or Track related at the top of Trends or in Map settings → Your data. The choice applies to both the map and statistics for the current session. Filter or scope changes clear old map markers and refresh media results; stale requests cannot restore the old selection. An explicitly opened activity’s own media timeline remains an activity detail view. Health retains its separate data range. ## Implementation MediaTrendQueryRepository owns the track interval and media capture-time predicate used by bounds, trend and item queries. All three APIs require matching trackIds in both scopes. ALL_INDEXED remains the API enum value for the All media choice; it now means all media within the result-defined interval. The map bounds endpoint uses POST to carry large track selections. An empty ID list returns an empty result; a missing list is invalid. Synthetic database integration tests cover continuous gaps, inclusive boundaries, old/future/undated media, selected links, capture-time corrections, empty selections, and agreement between bounds, counts and browsing. Frontend tests cover ID forwarding, shared scope, aligned charts, totals, and stale request cancellation.

title: Media indexing
text: # Media indexing Media indexing reads file metadata and retains capture time, embedded location, source identity, and technical properties. The original file remains the source for downloads and content conversion. Original contents are hashed as a stream for common source issues . Content failures keep account acknowledgements across unchanged retries. Empty files finish as informational skips and retain any earlier imported records. Import and metadata changes remain transactional; unexpected service failures keep operational recovery separately from source acceptance. GPS and media have separate scan/watch policies; their shipped defaults and manual rescan actions are in background processing . The format registry defines recognized image and video extensions. Metadata extraction and content decoding still depend on the format and packaged tools. Index changes enqueue correlation work. Resized previews and video streams are requested separately from metadata indexing. Content freshness and source revisions prevent obsolete content from becoming current results. The shared GPS/media file indexer commits each directory discovery in an independent transaction. Failed writes remain for the next scan. Watcher events coalesce on a separate discovery thread. Every source is committed before import dispatch. SCHEDULED is the durable discovered/unprocessed queue; PROCESSING is committed before the consumer starts. Discovery does not wait for imports. Progress counts include the full committed backlog, and the UI shows discovery separately while its total is still growing. Directory scans compare at most 256 source identities at a time using narrow database projections. Full index entities are loaded only for state changes. Scans retain counts rather than complete changed-file or missing-file lists. After discovery commits, pending work is read by increasing file ID in batches of 128; each batch finishes before the next is dispatched. The database retains the full backlog while scan memory stays bounded. Missing sources are checked in a separate paged pass after a complete directory walk. Work is serialized per path through completion persistence; a stored generation rejects superseded callbacks. Discovering another revision during active work persists RESCHEDULED without replacing that consumer's source snapshot. The start callback preserves this status; the older completion returns it to SCHEDULED for the next revision instead of marking the file completed. lastSuccessfulGeneration is a processing attempt number, not a timestamp; it allows an unchanged restoration to cancel removal before cleanup starts. File attributes are refreshed when work starts. Consumers check the source revision before committing and roll back and queue the latest revision when it changes. Successful completion follows the domain-data commit; independent completion writes retry failures, and restart/rescan safely replays orphaned work. Committed discovery survives a failed import or a lost dispatch notification. Missing-source cleanup requires an accessible source root and confirmed absence. Incomplete walks do not dispatch removals. Failed cleanup remains visible as failed work; REMOVED records successful cleanup. Original files are read only. Location projection, time correction, and activity correlation are distinct stored concerns. A manually assigned location does not rewrite EXIF. See correlation , selection , and delivery . The media runtime owns native packages and their checks.

title: Route planning
text: # Route planning The planner keeps an editable client draft with waypoints, profile, route legs, and local points of interest. Request generations and cancellation prevent stale routing responses from replacing newer edits. The server calls BRouter and returns route geometry and statistics. Saved plans retain their payload in the existing planner storage. They remain separate from imported GPS activities and their statistics. Saving waits for current geometry and retains user input on failure. Reopening a plan restores its route and places. GPX export contains route geometry; POI-only plans have no route export. Public trail and place overlays are visual references. They do not silently supply route waypoints or visiting-order optimization. POI optimization research remains internal. See planner source , BRouter service , and the user procedure . Points of interest use unique UUID identifiers. Persistence validates coordinates, name length, notes, and supported icons; the client supplies the identifiers.

title: Processing status and dependencies
text: # Processing status and dependencies GET /api/status?include=processing collects domain-owned job reports. The status collector contains no workflow prerequisites or job-specific counting queries. Each ProcessingJob owns its report, declared dependency edges, and prerequisite evaluation. Execution and reporting call the same evaluation. Shared import barriers live with their job consumers in ImportPrerequisites, rather than in status collection. ## Live reports Existing outcome counts and percentages remain available. Additional fields provide the server-selected state, work.ready, work.waiting, work.retrying, blockedBy, nextRunAt, nextRetryAt, unit, and progressKnown. Ready includes eligible items currently executing; it is not a count of worker threads. The three work counts partition pending work. Source limitations and attention counts remain separate from execution state. The shared policy chooses Running while a batch executes; otherwise Queued when any work is ready, Retrying when any work is deferred for retry, Waiting when any work awaits prerequisites, and Complete when no work remains. An active whole-job gate also reports Waiting before upstream discovery has established any pending count. Unknown totals use progressKnown=false. Blockers identify an index, job, lock, or user action, with whole-job or item scope and Automatic or User-action resolution. Lock blockers report the current owner. Classification awaiting duplicate checks and energy awaiting classification are ordinary waits. A completed classification with no activity requires user action. Exploration applies its gate to the entire pending count without querying point eligibility for every pending track. Media duplicate changes are retriggers, rather than a whole-job blocking prerequisite. A request memoizes shared import facts. Existing database aggregates gain filtered counts where possible. Current gates are evaluated on every poll; last batch results are not used as a stale prerequisite cache. ## Execution and scheduling BackgroundJobRunner distinguishes ownership of a continuation chain from execution. A domain batch signals its start after gates and work selection; execution is cleared in a finally block. Heavy batches obtain the shared resource lock before entering this execution scope. Typed batch outcomes preserve blockers or retry times while controlling continuation scheduling. nextRunAt describes a scheduled check or an immediate continuation. It is registered at application startup and is not a promised start time. An occupied resource lock or scheduler can delay execution. Runtime markers remain in memory; work and retry deadlines remain in the database. Counts and markers can cross a commit boundary, so an executing batch may briefly have zero pending items. ## Dependency metadata and GUI Each enabled provider advertises Gate, Input, or Retrigger edges. The collector returns them once at the top level of Processing, with an opaque dependenciesVersion. A caller can pass that version in later requests; unchanged edges are omitted while live reports are still returned. The client keeps the cached graph and replaces it when its version changes. The GUI displays server-selected states with distinct icons, visible blocker reasons, linked rows, and a compact dependency section inside each job's Details. Attention is an independent badge. Servers without the added state fields retain the previous client presentation. Indexer rows and map/routing services keep their existing state contracts. Task counts play confirmed samples eight seconds behind the shared status clock, with a local render tick every 400 ms. Each row uses one completed count to keep its summary, pending count, ready work, details, and meter in step. Stable totals and outcomes allow playback; changed totals, outcomes, blockers, execution state, or decreasing completed counts reset it immediately. Finished work also settles immediately. Reduced motion shows the latest sample; hidden views pause their render tick, and reopening reuses the shared timeline. Polling remains unchanged. Synthetic Google Health advertises its import, duplicate detection, activity classification, and energy gates through its own provider. It appears under Imports & sync, reports preparation before day totals are known, publishes committed day progress, and reports automatic retry times.

title: Replay architecture
text: # Replay architecture Single-track replay requires loaded route geometry. Recording gaps do not block replay; positions between available points are interpolated. Supported canonical timing drives playback when available, with distance-based playback for missing, unreliable or estimated timing. Distance-based playback does not derive an activity duration from unsupported timing. trackReplayController.ts owns the playback clock; trackReplayPath.ts supplies sampled positions. replayCameraRailPlanner.ts prepares a duration-aware camera rail. trackReplayCamera.ts samples it, while viewport and screen guards keep the route subject visible around UI occlusion. Playback consumes that plan instead of rebuilding analytical metrics in the browser. Segment replay uses server-resolved exact attempt geometry and timing. Comparison and replay share attempt identities, labels, colors, and supported inspected positions. Recording breaks and unsupported timing remain unavailable. Archive animation is a separate date-based display of activities. It does not replay point timing along a single track. See single-track source , segment replay , and the server contract .

title: Source issues and acknowledgements
text: # Source issues and acknowledgements GPS diagnosis and media ingest publish issues through SourceIssueRepository. source_issue identifies a semantic defect by source, content revision, and finding hash. Readable revisions use streamed SHA-256 of original contents. Unreadable episodes persist one UUID until reading succeeds. File size, modification time, message wording, retries, and rounded measurements are not acknowledgement identities. Domain severity escalation changes the finding hash. REVIEW issues require acceptance. INFORMATION includes empty-file skips and the GPS assessment-limit exception. Incomplete assessment remains explicit and does not resolve unchecked stages. Complete stages resolve absent findings; readable changed contents resolve the older revision. Removal resolves history while retaining indexed_file; hard deletion and database reset cascade through issues and acknowledgements. source_issue_acknowledgement stores one current row per issue and canonical authenticated account name. Duplicate inserts preserve the timestamp; Reopen deletes the row. Login case variants share a key. Account renaming starts a new scope. Shared demo credentials share acknowledgements; browser cleanup does not clear them. track_review_decision stores shared map/statistics choices and their actor separately. Review later stores nothing. No legacy issue backfill is run. The targets endpoint returns a complete immutable selection of issue IDs and revisions in one read transaction. Its default state is PENDING; state=ACKNOWLEDGED returns the complete selection for Reopen, including issues beyond the visible page. pendingFileCount is zero for an acknowledged selection. Per-file acknowledgement uses the issue revisions displayed in Review. Bulk actions show the snapshot's file and issue counts before submitting that selection once. One transaction validates active reviewable rows under existing source guards and applies set-based writes in bounded batches. New, changed, resolved, or excluded targets are not accepted by old requests. The result includes changed/already-acknowledged/stale counts, exact changedTargets, and account source summaries. Undo reopens only those newly acknowledged targets, preserving acknowledgements another device saved before the submission. A failure rolls back all batches. Writes are not automatically retried. The client serializes issue actions and updates shared summaries only after a confirmed response. Older in-flight status reads cannot restore superseded pending counts. Feedback survives list refresh and navigation. Failed Undo keeps its targets and a retry action. Navigation is disabled during submission; per-file advance requires the current source to have no pending issues. Reassessment refreshes diagnosis and its issue controls together. Cross-device opposite actions follow database write order. Map, Review, Processing, and overview summaries count distinct pending files, including imported GPS quality findings. Raw processing totals and operational failures remain separate. Acknowledgement cannot repair data or make timing reliable. There is no browser acknowledgement token or freshness snooze. Stable zero-byte GPS/media files finish as SKIPPED, distinct from configured EXCLUDED. Normal content changes queue them again. Existing imported records are retained; the current empty-source explanation identifies this. Content failures remain reviewable; unexpected import/service failures retain operational recovery. See Processing .

title: System architecture
text: # System architecture MTL Explorer serves a Vue PWA and Spring Boot API under /mtl/. PostgreSQL with PostGIS stores tracks, derived data, plans, corrections, and optional Health records. Original GPS and media files stay in mounted folders. ## Responsibilities | Component | Owns | | --- | --- | | Server | Ingest, domain calculations, filtering, transactions, jobs, API contracts | | Browser | Selection, display, input conversion, charts, map rendering, local preferences and caches | | Database | Authoritative stored records, work state, spatial indexes, user changes | | Source folders | Original files needed for downloads and normal reimport | | Routing and search services | Routing geometry and location lookup | | Map service | Archive delivery; server selects and proxies the upstream | GPS ingestion runs conversion, canonical processing, indexing, and downstream jobs. Media correlation consumes supported track timing. Health synchronization maintains separate records and can publish exercise routes to normal GPS import. Saved plans stay separate from imported activity statistics. The database relation diagrams show table keys and relationships. API types come from the exported OpenAPI schema . Browser caches must follow server revisions; neither map simplification nor chart reduction owns analytical totals. External map, terrain, trail, account, and update services have separate availability. A browser cache and a server-local map archive do not make all calculations available offline. See GPS processing , segment calculations , media correlation , Health sync , and caching . Deployment services and mounts are defined by Compose .

title: Measurement systems and API units
text: # Measurement systems and API units Persistence and domain calculations use canonical metric values. The browser converts values for display and converts user input back to the declared unit. Locale and measurement system are independent. ## Presentation | System | Distance | Elevation | Speed | Vertical rate | Mass | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Metric | km or m | m | km/h | m/h | kg | | Imperial (US) | mi or ft | ft | mph | ft/h | lb | Watts, watt-hours, time, percentages, and coordinates do not change. The browser resolves an explicit preference first, then the server default, then browser language/timezone detection. The fallback is Metric. Use default removes the explicit preference; it is not another API enum value. useMeasurementSystem.ts owns preference resolution. units.ts owns shared conversions and formatting. Unit changes do not reinterpret persisted filter values. ## API contract The exported schema defines actual property names. Current names include trackLengthInMeter, radius, and distance_meters; these have not all been renamed to a common suffix convention. Most analytical requests use their declared canonical unit. An operation receives measurementSystem only when the domain definition changes, such as milestone thresholds. Statistics Overview returns the system whose milestone profile was evaluated. Supported enum values are METRIC and US_CUSTOMARY. SQL filter parameters retain their declared metadata units. Distance filters can use km and energy filters kWh. The filter conversion helper converts supported controls to those declared units. Do not substitute meters or Wh just because other API fields use them. ## Server-owned milestones MeasurementSystemService owns profiles and converts their thresholds to canonical values. | Profile | Distance milestones | Ascent milestones | Energy milestone | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Metric | 10, 25, 50, 100 km | 500, 1,000, 2,000 m | 1,000 Wh | | US customary | 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 mi | 1,000, 2,500, 5,000 ft | 1,000 Wh | The server queries the earliest qualifying track for each definition. A 100-mile milestone uses exactly 160,934.4 m and can select a different activity from the 100-km milestone. The browser must not derive one milestone profile from another. The shared model uses MeasurementSystem, MeasurementConversions, MilestoneDimension, MilestoneDefinition, and MilestoneProfile. Milestone responses carry canonical meter or Wh thresholds and achieved values. The generated client renders these fields; it does not reconstruct thresholds. Broader API renames and dynamic unit/dimension metadata remain proposals. They are separate from this implemented contract.

title: Development
text: # Development Start with the development setup . Java builds and tests run inside the existing development container. | Topic | Reference | | --- | --- | | Server | Backend , GPS diagnostics module , profiling | | Client | Frontend , styling | | API | Schema export and client generation | | Verification | Testing | | Plans | Google Health synchronization plan , ingest issue acknowledgement plan | | Packaging | Container builds , release workflow | | Public site | Website and documentation | Read Architecture before changing domain ownership. Follow repository instructions and contribution guidance . ## Shared code rules Use named constants for semantic, reused, or tunable values. Avoid production magic numbers and strings. Reuse existing constants and keep new ones in the smallest useful scope. ## Software versions Verify the latest stable non-beta release before proposing or pinning software, runtime, package, or base-image versions. Prefer the latest stable LTS release unless compatibility requires an older version.

title: API schema and client generation
text: # API schema and client generation OpenAPI is the API type source of truth. Change the server first, then export its live schema and regenerate the TypeScript client. Never hand-edit API shapes. Add JSON fields in thematic Java order and match @JsonPropertyOrder. ## Export the schema With the development backend running, work from mtl-api/open-api-schema/: Check both commands succeeded before replacing schema.json. Keep two-space indentation, original field order, a trailing newline, and the normal http://localhost:8080/mtl server URL. Remove the temporary files afterward. Configure the export server correctly rather than editing the exported values. ## Generate the client Inside the existing Java development container, run from mtl-api/: The generated package is under mtl-api-typescript-fetch/target/generated-sources/mtl-typescript/. Its source and compiled output are build artifacts. The frontend manifest consumes that package through its local file: dependency. Run npm install in mtl-client/ after the first generation. Finish regeneration before starting Vite after Maven clean. Use generated models and API methods. Document any temporary generator workaround, and verify relevant backend/frontend contracts after a shape change. Run relevant backend/frontend checks and report pre-existing failures separately. The saved schema defines actual field names and units; architecture explains semantics.

title: Backend development
text: # Backend development The Spring Boot application lives in mtl-server/. Maven owns compilation, packaging, and tests. Run these commands inside the existing development container, from mtl-server/: The diagnostics module compiles during the Maven lifecycle and is required at runtime. Use the configured module path; see GPS diagnostics . Use an isolated database and public/synthetic data for tests. Follow the testing guide and preserve pre-existing failures separately from results for the change. After API changes, export the live schema and regenerate the client through the API workflow . Source and runtime settings are owned by the POM and application configuration. ## Implementation Keep advanced domain calculations on the server. Change APIs rather than duplicating calculation logic in the client. Prefer existing repositories and standard framework features over separate persistence helper classes. Format code and organize Java imports using the project style. Limit cleanup to code changed for the task. Follow shared code rules and software version policy . ## Logging Log major server operations and lifecycle phases at INFO: start, meaningful milestones or phase summaries, completion, duration, and useful counts. Keep per-record and other high-volume detail at DEBUG. Log every caught exception with operation context, its type, and a safe message before recovering, falling back, or returning. Do not silently ignore exceptions or use empty catch blocks. Use WARN for recoverable failures and ERROR with the throwable when the operation fails. Keep repeated recoverable stack traces at DEBUG to avoid flooding normal logs. ## Data migration Do not add legacy-data backfills or old-data migration paths unless explicitly requested. Assume users can recreate the database after derived-statistic or data-shape changes. Keep ingest and recalculation for new imports; avoid migration-only administration endpoints and services.

title: Home Container Build
text: # Home Container Build For the normal installation path with prebuilt images, follow the README quick start . This page is only for building MTL Explorer Docker images locally from a source checkout. The container build runs the Maven reactor inside Docker. That includes OpenAPI TypeScript client generation and the Vue production build. It creates images in your local Docker daemon; it does not replace normal Maven, npm, IDE, or frontend dev-server workflows. Run Java/Maven development commands inside the existing development container; do not run the backend on the host. The runtime includes the Spring Boot application JAR and the named GPS diagnostics module JAR. Custom launchers must preserve their module-path arguments; see GPS quality modules . The app installs precompiled libvips, ImageMagick, FFmpeg and libheif from conda-forge. Image previews use libvips first, with a logged and signaled ImageMagick fallback when libvips has no native loader for the input format. Separate AMD64 and ARM64 lock files pin every package and SHA-256 checksum. The runtime build checks the public iOS 18 HEIC regression, video thumbnails and H.264/AAC streaming. See media packages and tests for versions, lock updates and focused build commands. GPSBabel still builds from source. The Garmin installer uses bsdtar (libarchive-tools) for source archives. Ubuntu 26.04's GNU tar can fail with Function not implemented when extracting nested paths in amd64 builds under OrbStack/Rosetta; see OrbStack issue 2588 . ## Images The examples build: - mytraillog:local - app image - mytraillog-brouter:local - BRouter image - mytraillog-location-search:local - GeoNames search sidecar image - mytraillog-maps:local - optional local map sidecar image These names are local Docker tags only; the product name is MTL Explorer. ## Build and run Run from the repository root, where docker-compose.yml is located. macOS, Linux, WSL, or Git Bash: Windows PowerShell: For useful local location search, build docker-location-search/geonames-search/build/geonames-search.sqlite first or mount your own database at ./data/location-search/geonames-search.sqlite. The MTL_*_IMAGE variables tell Compose to use local images instead of the published defaults. MTL_IMAGE_PULL_POLICY=never prevents Compose from trying to pull those local-only tags. After startup, use the same URL, login, data folders, and update commands described in Administration . ## Publishing an app release Commit source changes, increment APP_VERSION_TAG in docker-build-deploy.py, and commit that version before running ./docker-build-deploy.py --yes --app-only. This publishes the version and alpha for AMD64 and ARM64; add --dry-run to preview. App releases build from a fixed Git archive, excluding uncommitted run evidence. The helper rejects other pending changes and existing app version tags, embeds the full Git revision and tree in image labels and manifest annotations, and records their image digest in the private checkout's docs-my/operations/releases/builds/ directory. Commit the app record mytraillog-BUILD.json and component manifest mtl-bundle-BUILD.json there. These small records are durable release metadata, kept outside the public source checkout. The digest identifies the exact built image; the Git revision identifies its source, not downloaded dependencies. The default private checkout is ../mtl-explorer-private; MTL_PRIVATE_REPO overrides its location. Without that checkout, pass --release-record-dir /path/to/private-release-records to choose a persistent directory outside the application checkout. The helper shows the directory in its plan, checks it before publishing, and refuses to overwrite existing records. Dry runs write nothing. Channel-only promotion uses the existing images and does not require a record directory. Old files under logs/releases/ are historical; use the records generated for the tested build. About shows the revision baked into the frontend, and Settings → System information shows the server's revision from MTL_IMAGE_REVISION or /opt/mtl/image-revision. Both show an eight-character hash beside the version; click it to reveal the full revision. System information offers “Copy all versions” with a preview of client, server, database, runtime, and sidecar versions. The report excludes logs, configuration, URLs, paths, and installation identifiers. Builds without revision metadata show the version alone. Read the revision with docker buildx imagetools inspect wauwau0977/mytraillog:alpha, then compare source with git diff <image-revision> HEAD in this workspace. Use image@sha256:… when a test must keep using the same image as a channel moves. ## Optional local map image Build and use the map sidecar image only if you want to test the local map container too: The local-maps profile downloads about 130 GB of map data on first startup. For the simpler hosted-map setup, leave this profile disabled and follow the README quick start .

title: Frontend development
text: # Frontend development The Vue, TypeScript, MapLibre, and PrimeVue PWA lives in mtl-client/ and is served under /mtl/. Generate the API package in the development container first, then run from mtl-client/: Vite proxies /mtl/api to the local backend. Set VITE_DEV_PROXY_TARGET when using another backend address. The development service worker is disabled. ## User flows Design the complete user flow before editing UI code; avoid narrow visual patches. Follow the shared controls, panel behavior, and typography in the styling guide , and keep changes consistent across the flow. Domain calculations belong to the server; follow backend ownership . Use generated API types and shared code rules . ## Stable test identifiers Give major actions, navigation, inputs, panels, and important result/error states stable data-test IDs. Add them during development and when filling regression gaps. Decorative elements need none. Use purpose-based names, such as planner-save-plan, stable across layout, theme, and language changes. Put action IDs on interactive DOM elements in production builds. Scope repeated controls by stable item keys, not list positions. Keep accessible names and labels; test IDs supplement them. Update affected tests when changing IDs. Follow the browser locator rules . ## Profiling and checks For browser profiling, use profile mode. It keeps the production runtime and chunk layout, disables JavaScript and CSS minification, includes source maps, and disables service worker generation and registration. Set MTL_PROFILE_DIR to a dedicated output directory on your data drive, then run: Open /mtl/ on that port. Use a fresh origin or clear any existing service worker before recording. Unminified assets increase load size; compare final load timings with a normal production build. Available checks: Run npm run format to format client source, tests, and configuration with the project Prettier settings. build includes type checking; build-only only bundles assets. Edit source and public/, then rebuild. Do not edit copied server assets or dist/. The manifest owns scripts and dependencies. Read styling , API generation , and documentation authoring . ## Errors and diagnostics Rethrow the original caught value with throw error. Do not replace it with new Error(String(error)): that loses its type, stack, HTTP response, and cancellation metadata. If a distinct user-facing message requires a wrapper, use new Error(message, { cause: error }) and retain the original failure. Report the original transport error before reading private response details for the UI. Keep credentials, response bodies, and private application values out of diagnostics. Use startupLog and startup timer success for normal startup, progress, and sign-in transitions. Reserve warnings and errors for problems. Pass the actual failure as the third argument to startupWarn / startupError, or the second argument to timer warn / error; pass structured context separately after it. Use undefined for the error when a warning has only context. Context objects and timing metadata are not exceptions. See diagnostic logging .

title: Development setup
text: # Development setup Use the existing checkout and Java development container. On this machine the running container is mtl-java-dev; start it on demand if stopped. Do not install Java or run Maven on the host. 1. Inspect git status and preserve unrelated changes. 2. In the development container, generate the TypeScript API package . 3. Build and run the backend with its diagnostics module. 4. Start the frontend from mtl-client/. 5. Use the printed /mtl/ URL in the Codex in-app browser. Obtain local GUI credentials only from mtl-server/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml. 6. Run checks relevant to the change. Keep trial datasets and raw evidence on the mounted external drive. Use public or fully synthetic data. Stop temporary instances after checks and retain downloaded map/routing data. ## Build script Run the build script from the repository root: The script builds a verified source snapshot in the development container and keeps outputs, build.log, and build.json on the mounted external drive. It accepts compile, test, package, and verify; put wrapper flags before the action and Maven options after --. By default, the script generates and installs the TypeScript API package from the saved schema, packages the Vue client into the snapshot's server resources, then runs the requested server goal. The API build supplies its configured Node/npm toolchain. --client-only generates the API package and runs the requested client Maven goal. --server-only skips the API and client steps. Server-only packages contain no bundled UI; use the default build for a complete application. Maven options apply to the server when included, otherwise to the client. Client Maven goals use the existing build-only task, which does not run TypeScript checks or client tests. Source files in the checkout are not updated. Snapshots are retained by default. For disposable builds, put --keep N before the action to retain the newest N successful disposable snapshots per checkout and selected component. Cleanup only considers snapshots created with --keep; existing, failed, running, and other checkouts' snapshots are retained. Create a .keep file inside a snapshot to pin it. Omit --keep for saved verification evidence. Cleanup runs after a successful build.

title: Google Health synchronization implementation plan
text: # Google Health synchronization implementation plan Status: implemented and verified locally 10 October 2026. Simplify automatic historical imports to ordinary batch upserts and permanent day completion records. Reuse the existing audit table, record identities, durable work, and ownership guards. Keep recent synchronization behavior. The synchronization architecture describes the implementation. This plan remains the authority for the historical import contract and its acceptance checks. ## Scope and synchronization lanes | Lane | Range and schedule | Record writes | | --- | --- | --- | | Recent fast | Last physical 24 hours, every cycle, with existing civil/date envelopes | Complete-chunk upsert and replacement | | Recent full | Non-final part of the seven-day recent window; due 24 hours after completion, resumed while unfinished | Complete-chunk upsert and replacement | | Historical | Eligible unmarked days before the recent cutoff, newest first, down to the configured floor | Batch upsert, then one successful audit mark per day and stream | Keep current defaults: a 30-minute cycle, a seven-day recent window, a 24-hour fast window, a 24-hour full-pass interval, and a history floor of 2010-01-01. Preserve explicit installation settings and endpoint limits. Historical records are treated as fixed. Future upstream changes are outside the automatic synchronization contract and must not drive this implementation. A completed historical day is never automatically imported again. Recovery is explicit user maintenance, such as resetting the mirror and importing afresh. ## Logical days and completion records The logical unit is a native day for one account, data type, representation, calendar policy, and key policy. API pages, query subdivisions, and database batches are execution details. Their sizes can change without changing which days are complete. Retain the existing key and calendar policy versions; a write optimization must not rekey records or reopen completed days. Retain the existing native time rules and half-open [start, end) bounds: | Stream | Day ownership | | --- | --- | | Physical samples and intervals | UTC day of the sample or interval start | | Exercise | Civil start day | | Sleep | UTC end day; viewing still groups sessions by start day | | Daily summaries and rollups | Native date or aggregation day | Keep physical instants, civil components, and dates distinct. Use existing calendar policies, completion eligibility, civil envelopes, and microsecond precision. Recent work cannot commit below its current cutoff; historical work cannot finalize a day that is still recent-owned. Use google_health.history_audit as the completion authority. Its existing partial unique index allows one active successful record per scoped day. | Outcome | Meaning | | --- | --- | | DATA | Every required query and page succeeded; at least one valid record was returned for the day and all writes are committed | | EMPTY | Every required query and page succeeded and returned no records | | Failed or absent | The day is incomplete | Determine DATA versus EMPTY from that day's current successful traversals, including returned records already stored. Zero new inserts or updates does not mean EMPTY. Earlier failed or restarted traversals do not determine the outcome. EMPTY describes the query result; it neither asserts that no local rows exist nor authorizes their deletion. Failed attempts may have audit entries, but never count as completion. Gaps between measurements are valid. Completion means that every required query and page succeeded, not that every instant has a measurement. An empty page with a continuation token is not a completed query. A backward watermark is only a cached summary of contiguous completed days. For each stream, start at the newest eligible day and stop at the first incomplete day. It never replaces the day audit lookup. Do not infer completion from record timestamps, counts, or old cursors. ## Historical import flow 1. Select or resume the newest eligible incomplete day. Before requesting it, check the scoped audit. Skip DATA and EMPTY permanently during automatic synchronization, including after restart or downtime. 2. Reuse durable work with frozen query bounds and an ownership generation. Query subdivisions cover the whole day without gaps or overlaps. Keep one active historical owner per account and logical stream. 3. Fetch and validate one page. Normalize its records once, resolve sources inside the guarded transaction, and write them in ordinary batches. 4. Commit the page records, next-page checkpoint, query-validation state, counts, and historical rotation together. Verify account, current ownership, day eligibility, and absence of a successful audit at every commit. Follow every continuation token. Earlier committed pages survive a later failure or interruption. 5. After all required subdivisions and pages succeed, use a short guarded transaction to write the successful day audit and complete its work. Completion performs no mirror scan, record stamping, or absence deletion. Retain bounded empty-range batching where supported. Each covered day still receives its own completion record. A shared request or write batch never becomes the completion unit. Shared requests include only contiguous eligible days and exclude completed, waiting, parked, or separately owned days. Older eligible days can still progress beyond a failed gap; that gap stays incomplete. ## Historical record writes Start with batched INSERT … ON CONFLICT through the existing repositories. Insert all validated returned records. If the identity already exists, reuse its row and update content only when it differs. Identical retries must produce the same stored result without rewriting unchanged rows. A row already stored by an earlier import is an upsert conflict. Conflicting duplicates within the current query are a validation failure; these are different cases. Remove these operations from the automatic historical path: - Per-record traversal stamps and writes made solely to record query membership. - Absence sweeps and historical deletion or replacement of missing identities. - Separate database scans solely to calculate changed-record counts before writing; derive counts from persistence results where needed. - Repeated validation and mapping of the same page. Completion and retry safety do not depend on per-record stamps. Retain traversal IDs in work/checkpoint state for request resumption and ownership checks. Keep the existing input and identity safeguards: - Accept a Google name as identity only when it is a complete users/{user}/dataTypes/{type}/dataPoints/{point} resource matching the type. A collection path cannot identify a record. - Preserve the current canonical fallback for nameless records. Different observations at the same time remain distinct, including when source metadata is missing or identical. - Reconciled and rollup identities remain independent of page and batch sizes. - Collapse identical duplicate identities. Reject conflicting content for the same identity within one query, including across pages and resumed work. - Reject invalid payloads, times, and out-of-range records before their page commits. Source caches remain scoped and are invalidated on rollback/reset. For named and other content-independent identities, keep the identity/fingerprint state needed for cross-page validation in durable query work. Commit it with the page checkpoint, restore it on resume, and discard it when that traversal is restarted, revoked, or completed. Identities that already include the canonical observation fingerprint need no separate conflict state. Keep this state within the existing query limits; it contains no second copy of record payloads and requires no mirror membership stamps or scans. Use ordinary batching against the existing mirror tables. Separate record staging tables and a storage redesign are outside this change. Heart-rate indexes separate named from nameless identity. Complete Google names keep a unique (connection_id, identity_key) index, so a correction can move one row in time. Nameless keys already include the physical time and canonical observation; their unique index is (connection_id, sample_time, identity_key). Recent and maintenance lookups pass the sample time for nameless records. This keeps writes near the current time range while preserving key values and logical uniqueness. Unused mirror fingerprint indexes are removed. ## Interruption and failure handling A transaction failure rolls back its records and checkpoint together. On restart, resume the last committed checkpoint. A replayed page is safe because writes use the existing unique identities. A reset, reload, or retry that replaces ownership revokes stale generations. Old workers cannot commit pages, advance checkpoints, or write successful day marks. The final audit and work completion are atomic; a failed finalization leaves the day incomplete. Keep existing bounded retries, waiting/parked states, and token handling. A structured INVALID_PAGE_TOKEN restarts the affected subdivision under a new traversal and smaller bounds where possible. Do not reuse a token after changing its request. Repeated tokens or unrecoverable requests leave work incomplete. Parked work does not prevent older eligible days from progressing; contiguous coverage still stops at the gap. Budget yields, cancellation, quota pauses, and authorization pauses are not work failures. Page memory and write batches remain bounded. ## Existing behavior to preserve Recent fast/full passes continue to fetch complete chunks, skip unchanged content, and replace absent identities within their exact queried bounds. They retain frozen full-pass positions, retries, cutoff handoff, and due times. Successful historical days remain excluded even if the recent window widens. Keep the serialized worker, fixed-rate schedule, lane reservations, stream rotation, shared request limiter, and durable cooldown. Scheduling budgets control admission of another request or finalization. An admitted page saves under the independent database transaction timeout; it must not repeatedly roll back merely because its scheduling slice expired. Explicit range/all reload remains user-requested maintenance with its existing replacement contract. Keep that maintenance path separate from automatic historical imports. Only explicit maintenance supersedes successful day marks; retrying incomplete work does not reopen completed days. Full reset clears mirror records, audits, work, failures, passes, and caches under the guard. Reload intent is a range audit with outcome RELOAD_REQUESTED, never a successful day mark. Historical work freezes its replace_missing mode from that intent; the request also survives a recent-to-history handoff. Same-account reauthorization preserves marks and work. Empty audits and route ownership still protect account identity; another account requires an explicit reset. Zero mirror rows never imply a reset. Route exports remain separate from record completion. Keep route ownership, published files, and track associations. Automatic synchronization does not delete published routes, and adding location permission does not reopen historical days. ## Status and measurement Expose per-stream completed days, active day, pending/parked work, attempts, retry time, and contiguous coverage. Include empty completed days. Use indexed audit lookups and cached coverage; status polling and page commits must not scan the full audit table or mirror. Report fetched records and persisted changes separately. Derive changes from write results, never from fetched counts. If an exact count is unavailable, report that rather than adding a count query or inventing a value. Keep legacy stamp/deletion counters at zero for automatic history; do not reuse them to classify day outcomes. Cycle counts cover commits in that cycle; cumulative work counts survive restart. Use the import simulator to compare the old and new implementations with identical datasets, storage, and settings. Use a fixed dataset for historical imports; correction/removal cases belong to recent synchronization or explicit maintenance. Compare expected records and day audits as well as elapsed time. Measure: - Historical import time per day, database/transaction time, rows per second, page counts, and commit counts. - Active processing time separately from total elapsed time, including scheduling waits and retries. - Recent fast/full completion while historical work is pending. - Indexed work selection and status cost with a long history floor and gaps. Simulator transaction time covers work inside transactions. Page normalization occurs before automatic historical writes, so compare total elapsed time too. The simulator does not establish Google network latency or NAS disk throughput. Use existing NAS measurements for those operational comparisons. Do not claim a throughput target before measurement. An empty-mirror benchmark does not reproduce scattered index reads in a large existing mirror with a small database cache. Verify that workload separately; an individual lookup speedup is not a full-import speedup. Log useful phase durations and counts without health values, payloads, tokens, credentials, or account/device/point identifiers. ## Implemented changes 1. Automatic history has its own persistence path, reusing validation, canonical identities, source resolution, and the existing repository. Recent replacement and explicit maintenance retain their separate behavior. 2. Batch upserts omit stamps, absence sweeps, pre-write count scans, and duplicate mapping. Retry and duplicate-conflict safeguards remain in place. 3. Days finish from durable query/page state and valid returned counts, using the existing audit table and unique index. Status retains day-level coverage. 4. Correctness and performance use the existing simulator and Java checks in the development container. 5. Architecture and user documentation describe this import contract. Use Liquibase only for required schema changes. No legacy backfill, identity migration, automatic reset, new repair feature, or live deployment is included. Change 104 adds maintenance mode and bounded query-validation/count state to existing work tables, plus an index for reload intent. Record tables, key policy, calendar policy, and successful audit uniqueness are unchanged. Change 105 replaces the global nameless heart-rate identity index with the time-based unique index and removes unused fingerprint indexes. It does not rekey records, backfill values, or reopen completed days. ## Acceptance checks - A dense, paginated day stores every expected record and one successful audit. A later automatic run makes no historical request for that completed day. - Valid empty days complete once and stay complete after restart. Measurement gaps do not prevent completion. - A day whose returned records already exist is DATA, not EMPTY. - Interruptions before a page commit, after it, and during finalization preserve consistent records/checkpoints. Resume adds no duplicate records or marks. - Invalid records, conflicting duplicates, repeated/expired tokens, and failed pages leave the day incomplete until a valid traversal succeeds. Cross-page conflict checks survive restart. Revoked workers cannot commit. - Parked gaps remain visible while older days progress. The backward watermark stops at the first gap. - Canonical identities preserve named records and differing same-time nameless observations. Fresh imports with different page or batch sizes produce equal records and day marks; existing completed days are never reopened by resizing. - Automatic history performs no traversal stamp updates or absence deletion. Completion cost depends on work/audit state, not all stored rows in the day. - Recent replacement, explicit reload/reset, account protection, route retention, quota handling, and budgeted continuation retain their behavior. - The benchmark produces the same expected records and completed days with lower historical persistence cost; timings distinguish processing from elapsed time.

title: GPS diagnostics module
text: # GPS diagnostics module Diagnostics is a named Java module in mtl-server. Its sources keep the com.x8ing.mtl.server.gpsquality.diagnostics package; its descriptor is in src/main/modules/diagnostics. The application depends on diagnostics; diagnostics depends only on the JDK. The repair module has been removed. GpxTimestampParser gives review and import the same strict clock interpretation. Missing offsets follow the GPX UTC convention and are logged as assumed UTC; original source text is retained. Import normalizes accepted values before JPX and leaves invalid timestamps absent without dropping geometry. Calendar overflow, leap seconds, excessive precision, and non-GPX offsets remain invalid; exact 24:00:00 means the next midnight. Maven compiles diagnostics during generate-sources and the application during compile. Separate output directories enforce the boundary even when tests are skipped. Lifecycle initialization clears module outputs and consumer .class files while preserving application resources, so incremental builds cannot retain removed modules or callers of removed APIs. Use lifecycle goals rather than direct compiler goals. mvn test uses the module path. GpsQualityModuleIsolationTest verifies runtime descriptors and rejects application dependencies. Enable GpsQualityModuleBuildIntegrationTest with -Dmtl.test.jpms.build=true to verify consumer recompilation without clean. mvn package produces the Boot JAR and the diagnostics JAR under target/gpsquality; Docker runs both. Core classes are excluded from the Boot JAR. Run Java commands in the existing development container. For a packaged run from mtl-server: Maven spring-boot:run is configured with the compiled module path. IDE launches require Maven compilation and equivalent VM arguments; startup rejects classpath-only diagnostics. Keep Spring, filesystem access and persistence in application adapters. Do not add module readability bypasses.

title: Ingest issue acknowledgement plan
text: # Ingest issue acknowledgement plan Status: implemented. Date: 11 October 2026. Current contracts: source issues architecture , Processing , and source review . The sections describing current behaviour below retain the pre-implementation design context. ## Problem MTL Explorer reports GPS and media import problems, including files that cannot be read or contain no usable data. Some problems are acceptable to the user, but the same files can keep drawing attention after the user has acknowledged them. Processing outcomes, GPS review decisions, and map notice dismissal do not share one model. ### Current behaviour | Mechanism | Meaning | Storage | | --- | --- | --- | | Map Acknowledge | Hide the current failed-file notice | Browser storage, scoped to server URL and account | | Map Minimize | Close the explanation and leave the compact indicator | Component state | | GPS Save use settings | Choose map/statistics inclusion and acknowledge current source findings | Server database | | Media failed-file list | Show filenames and saved errors | Server database, without per-file acknowledgement | The map acknowledgement survives ordinary logout and login in the same browser. It has no expiry timer. Clearing local application data removes it; another browser or device has its own acknowledgement. Processing, stale-map, offline, and unavailable-status notices remain independent. The map compares a saved token with the current GPS/media failure counts and the latest failed-file update timestamps. This records a processing snapshot, rather than a decision about the actual problems. Retrying the same bad file can restore the notice. Fixing or removing one file can also restore the notice for the remaining acknowledged files. GPS review already compares source content and meaningful findings. Cosmetic wording, ordering, and measurement rounding do not invalidate its decisions; new defects can require review even when the source bytes are unchanged. This review model does not control the map's processing-failure notice. A reviewed GPS source can therefore remain a failed file needing attention on the map, while an imported track with quality findings belongs to a separate queue. Acknowledgement is also coupled to GPS use settings. An empty source should not need a map/statistics exclusion choice merely to stop repeated notices. Conversely, acknowledging a timing problem cannot make its measurements reliable or rebuild a failed import. The client retains a five-minute freshness snooze and dismiss handler without a current UI caller. This adds an unused dismissal concept alongside the map notice. Settings → Processing derives its import Needs attention state from the raw failed-file count. A user can inspect failures but cannot acknowledge them there. Hiding the map notice therefore leaves the processing warning active. The user needs an action that clears accepted source problems consistently in both places, while preserving their processing outcomes and explanations. Current references: - Map notice and map status resolution . - Indexer summary and failure timestamp query . - GPS review persistence and finding identity . - Freshness store and map loading methods . - Processing progress and attention state and failed-file details . - Current processing guide and GPS review guide . ### Current database storage GPS decisions are stored in track_review_decision. Each save appends rows; the latest applicable row for a source revision and section determines its choice. This table currently combines use settings and acknowledgement. | Column | PostgreSQL type | Current meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | id | bigint, generated primary key | Decision history order | | source_id | bigint, foreign key to indexed_file.id | GPS source file | | source_hash | varchar(64) | Assessed source content hash | | finding_hash | varchar(64) | Semantic findings acknowledged by this choice | | section_index | integer | Source section, or -1 for an unsectioned source | | decision | varchar(24) | INCLUDE, EXCLUDE_MAP, EXCLUDE_STATISTICS, EXCLUDE, or LATER | | decided_at | timestamp with time zone | Time of the decision | All columns are non-null. An index covers (source_id, source_hash, section_index, id DESC). There is no account column; the choices apply to the shared library. track_source_review stores the GPS assessment, diagnosis JSON, and combined review state. The map acknowledgement has no database row; it remains in browser storage. See the existing table definitions . ## Plan Use one server-owned issue and acknowledgement model for GPS and media. Acknowledge one file or all current issues through the same operation. Keep processing outcomes and data-use choices separate from acknowledgement. ### Responsibilities | Layer | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Processing outcome | Record pending, imported, skipped, or failed work and its reason | | Issue | Describe a meaningful problem, its source revision, severity, and affected features | | Acknowledgement | Record that an account accepts leaving a particular issue as it is | | Use settings | Control whether available tracks contribute to the map and statistics | Acknowledgement does not change source files, processing outcomes, geometry, measurement reliability, or map/statistics use. Use settings remain library decisions; acknowledging issues is an account decision. Informational findings remain visible without requiring acknowledgement. Keep the existing GPS diagnosis engine, section inspection, and import evidence. Generalise the issue contract and acknowledgement bookkeeping, rather than adding a second acceptance mechanism only for failed indexed files. ### Database design Add two tables: source_issue for GPS/media issues and source_issue_acknowledgement for current account acknowledgements. Retain track_review_decision for map/statistics use only. The SQL below describes the proposed target schema; it is not an applied migration. #### Source issues One row represents one semantic defect in one source revision. A changed revision or meaningful defect creates a different row; updating explanatory wording or retry timestamps does not. source_id identifies the file through the existing indexer. Its GPS/media index and location remain in indexed_file; do not duplicate them here. source_revision is sha256:<content hash> for readable contents. For an unreadable source, persist an unreadable:<UUID> token for the continuous unreadable episode and reuse it across retries. It identifies that episode, not proven file contents. Once the file can be read, resolve the unreadable issue and assess its actual content revision. Do not use meta:<size>:<mtime> as a content identity. Metadata can be unavailable for unreadable sources, and changing modification time alone does not establish new contents. Available metadata can remain explanatory evidence in details. finding_hash identifies the semantic defect within that revision. details holds structured evidence such as affected point indices, counts, measurements, and affected features. The common issue table uses one normalized severity: REVIEW requires acknowledgement; INFORMATION does not. The server maps domain findings through its existing review policy. GPS warnings that require review map to REVIEW; the assessment-limit exception maps to INFORMATION while retaining its incomplete-assessment explanation. The original GPS severities remain in its diagnosis evidence. This mapping must not treat incomplete assessment as a healthy source. Keep meaningful domain changes, including severity escalation, in finding_hash even when their normalized severity is unchanged. There is no separate review_required column. A meaningful change in normalized severity belongs in the finding identity, so a newly reviewable defect cannot inherit a silent acknowledgement. An empty-file informational skip has reason EMPTY_FILE and severity INFORMATION. An issue is active while resolved_at is null. Repeated assessment upserts the same identity and updates its explanation and last_seen_at. Resolve absent findings only after a complete assessment of their relevant stage. A failed or limited assessment must not falsely resolve findings it could not check. Normal source removal retains the existing indexed_file row with status REMOVED and resolves its issues, preserving history. An explicit hard deletion or database reset removes the associated issues and acknowledgements through cascading foreign keys. This is distinct from clearing browser data. #### Current account acknowledgements Store only the current acknowledgement for each account and issue. A row means acknowledged; no row means pending when the issue is active and reviewable. Resolution belongs to source_issue, not to an account decision. account_key comes from the canonical authenticated server principal, not from a submitted username, browser identifier, JWT token, or login/session reference. Current authentication uses a configured account rather than a persistent user table, so use its canonical username without a session foreign key. Login case variants must produce the same key. Renaming that account creates a new scope; account renaming/migration is outside this change. Acknowledge inserts a row with ON CONFLICT (issue_id, account_key) DO NOTHING. Reopen deletes that row. Repeating either operation without an intervening opposite action is harmless. Keep the original acknowledged_at on duplicate inserts. No append-only acknowledgement history, request ID, or expected latest decision protocol is required. The primary key supports the per-issue account lookup; add further indexes only when query plans justify them. The primary key prevents duplicate acknowledgements; it does not order opposite user intentions. Concurrent Acknowledge and Reopen requests use ordinary database write ordering. A delayed Acknowledge processed after Reopen can acknowledge the issue again. The UI serializes opposite actions for the same issue while a request is pending, and the API does not add automatic mutation retries. Cross-device writes still follow server processing order. A stronger replay guarantee would require extra state and is outside this design. Keep the source/issue revision validation described below. It protects a different requirement: an old request must not acknowledge a new defect or source revision. Use the existing transactional source guards where needed; do not introduce a separate lock-ordering protocol for acknowledgement. There is no browser/device column, expiry column, or global accepted flag on indexed_file. Account scope is within this installation's database. A file with three reviewable issues gets three acknowledgement rows when acknowledged; the UI still counts it as one file. #### Shared demo account Current authentication configures one login in WebSecurityConfig . The demo login response supplies those same credentials to demo visitors. Visitors using that login therefore share one account: an acknowledgement by one visitor is visible to the others. Accept this shared behaviour for the current demo and clear the affected acknowledgements whenever its demo data is reset. Keep Acknowledge available. Separate visitor accounts or principals are a future authentication feature; do not substitute session identifiers for the account key in ordinary use. #### Map and statistics decisions Keep track_review_decision as the shared-library use-setting history, with this target shape: | Column | PostgreSQL type | Planned meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | id | bigint, generated primary key | Use-setting history order | | source_id | bigint, foreign key to indexed_file.id | GPS source file | | source_hash | varchar(64) | Source content revision the setting applies to | | section_index | integer | Existing source-section mapping | | decision | varchar(24) | INCLUDE, EXCLUDE_MAP, EXCLUDE_STATISTICS, or EXCLUDE | | decided_by | varchar(255) | Canonical account that saved the library setting | | decided_at | timestamp with time zone | Time of the setting | All target columns are non-null. Keep the existing latest-decision index and add a check constraint for the four use choices. Remove finding_hash from this table; acknowledgement lives only in source_issue_acknowledgement. Review later leaves issues pending and writes no use-setting row. A whole-source save retains the existing section mapping and writes choices for the affected sections. decided_by records the actor; it does not make use settings account-specific. The latest row for (source_id, source_hash, section_index) still controls the shared library. Existing track exclusion flags can remain projections of these choices. Refactor track_source_review.review_state and gps_track.review_status so they are not parallel authorities for an account's acknowledgement. Keep GPS diagnosis JSON as assessment evidence, with the common issue rows owning issue lifecycle and the acknowledgement rows owning review. #### State lookup and examples Derive the state for the authenticated account; do not save separate pending or accepted counters: | Issue row | Acknowledgement row for this account | Effective review state | | --- | --- | --- | | resolved_at is set | Present or absent | Resolved | | Active, severity INFORMATION | Present or absent | No acknowledgement required | | Active, severity REVIEW | Absent | Pending | | Active, severity REVIEW | Present | Acknowledged | For example, issue 101 is a GPS parsing failure for source 42, revision sha256:<hash A>. Synthetic current acknowledgement rows could look like this: | issue_id | account_key | acknowledged_at | | --- | --- | --- | | 101 | reviewer | 2026-10-11 12:00:00Z | | 101 | second-reviewer | 2026-10-11 12:02:00Z | Issue 101 is acknowledged for these accounts; an account without a row still sees it as pending. Reopen by reviewer deletes only (101, reviewer); the second account's acknowledgement remains. A retry with the same contents and defect keeps issue 101. If source 42 changes to revision sha256:<hash B> and still fails, create a new issue row without inheriting issue 101's acknowledgements. Older resolved findings retain their issue records and any remaining acknowledgement rows, but past Acknowledge/Reopen actions are not retained as an audit trail. The pending-file count uses active reviewable issues with no acknowledgement for the authenticated account: Bulk requests carry the exact issue IDs and source revisions in the displayed snapshot. Validate and write them transactionally; new or changed issues are not covered by the acknowledgement. ### Issue lifecycle and identity For each account, a reviewable issue is pending, acknowledged, or resolved. Acknowledgement persists on the server across logout, later logins, browser-data clearing, device changes, and server restarts. Another account retains its own pending issues. There is no automatic expiry. Use source identity, a content-based source revision, and a semantic defect identity. Reuse the GPS finding identity approach: stage, reason, severity, section, affected observations, and affected count where relevant. Adapt it to individual issues so removal of one defect does not invalidate acknowledgement of another. Size and modification time can trigger discovery, but do not alone prove that contents changed. Retry counters, processing timestamps, exception wording, finding order, and cosmetic measurement changes must not identify a new issue. Unreadable sources need an explicit revision representation without pretending that their contents were successfully assessed. | Event | Result | | --- | --- | | User acknowledges current issues | Those issue revisions become acknowledged for that account | | Logout/login, map reload, restart, or another device | Acknowledged issues stay quiet | | Retry or rescan finds the same defect in unchanged contents | Acknowledged issues stay quiet | | Another file is fixed, removed, or changed | Unrelated acknowledgements stay valid | | A particular problem disappears or its source is removed | That issue becomes resolved | | Changed source contents still have a reviewable problem | The new source revision requires review | | Assessment finds a new meaningful defect in unchanged contents | The new defect requires review; existing acknowledgements remain valid | | User selects Reopen | That account must review the selected issue again | A successful import resolves import failures that disappeared. It does not automatically resolve unrelated GPS quality findings. Acknowledged and resolved findings remain available with their explanations and current acknowledgement timestamps. Reopen removes the acknowledgement row; no acknowledgement action history is required. ### User flow - Review provides Acknowledge this file's issues for GPS and media. - The map provides Acknowledge all current issues for the issues represented by its current summary. - Settings → Processing provides the same overall Acknowledge all current issues action, covering current GPS and media source issues. Each import group also offers acknowledgement for that group's issues. - These actions preserve the findings and current use settings. Keep the term Acknowledge consistent; do not introduce a separate Accept action. - Review offers Pending and Acknowledged filters, diagnosis links, Reopen , and Retry where applicable. Retry schedules processing independently of acknowledgement; it does not automatically reopen an unchanged issue. - GPS retains separate whole-source and section map/statistics settings. Choosing Exclude does not implicitly replace issue acknowledgement. - Processing reports progress and outcomes, including informational skips, exposes per-file acknowledgement, and links to the same Review entries. - The map counts distinct files with pending reviewable issues, including quality findings in successfully imported sources. Multiple findings or affected calculations must not count the same source file repeatedly. - Minimize closes the explanation while leaving the compact indicator. It makes no saved review decision. Bulk acknowledgement must identify the source and issue revisions represented by the displayed summary or list. File IDs alone are insufficient. Issues that arrive or change while the request is in progress remain pending. Per-file requests must also reject stale issue revisions rather than acknowledge unseen findings. Repeated inserts or deletes are harmless without an intervening opposite action; concurrent opposite actions follow database write ordering. For example, acknowledge ten files with issues. An unchanged retry stays quiet. Fixing three files stays quiet. If one new file has an issue, the map reports one file needing review. ### Settings processing progress Make Needs attention actionable. Show the number of files with pending source issues and offer Review issues and Acknowledge all current issues on the Processing page. The overall action covers the whole library's current GPS and media issues, independently of map filters and list pagination. A GPS or media group action covers only that index. File details provide the same per-file action as Review. For source-related attention, derive the warning state from the current account's pending issues, not from raw failure totals. After acknowledgement, clear the source attention badge and warning styling once its pending count reaches zero. If pending issues remain or arrive later, keep Needs attention with the updated count. When processing has finished with no pending issues, show Complete · N files acknowledged if known issues remain; if work is still running, retain its running state and progress. Keep failed/skipped totals and their explanations visible as factual outcomes. Acknowledge does not increase the successful-import count. Calculations unavailable because of those same source issues must use the same acknowledgement when deciding whether to request attention. They can continue to show unavailable results and their reasons, without another persistent warning asking the user to accept the same limitation. Current operational failures keep their attention state and an appropriate recovery action. Update Processing, map, and Review summaries together from the bulk response. Only clear source attention after the server confirms the save. Disable overlapping acknowledgement/Reopen actions during submission and show a save failure without clearing warnings. No separate Processing dismissal state or extra acknowledgement table is needed. ### Bulk acknowledgement API Submit the complete selection in one request. Use the same endpoint for an overall action, one import group, selected files, or a single file; only the target array differs. The client must not call a per-file endpoint in a loop or submit only the currently visible list page. Provide a proposed snapshot endpoint: It returns the complete compact array of pending issue IDs and source revisions, with counts from that same snapshot. An optional index=GPS or index=MEDIA limits an import group action. The default includes all pending GPS/media source issues for the authenticated account. Obtain the array in one read when preparing the action; do not fetch every detail page or attach the full array to every progress poll. Display the snapshot counts and submit its targets without expanding the selection to later arrivals. Example snapshot response, with content hashes abbreviated for readability: The first two issues can belong to one GPS file and the third to a media file. Submit the full targets array to the proposed write endpoint: The server supplies account_key from Authentication.getName(). Deduplicate the targets and match them to active REVIEW issues with the exact submitted source revisions. Insert acknowledgements through a set-based INSERT … SELECT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING in one transaction. Do not perform one repository lookup/save or one source reassessment per target. Large input can use bounded internal SQL batches while retaining one client submission and one transaction. Return newly acknowledged, already acknowledged, and stale/resolved target counts, plus refreshed pending-file counts and GPS/media summaries for the current account. Stale or resolved targets are not acknowledged; other valid targets can still succeed. A database failure rolls back the whole write. If a per-file selection is entirely stale, show that its issues changed and refresh instead of claiming success. Issues arriving after the snapshot remain pending and appear in the returned summary. This needs no persisted bulk-operation record or request ID. The target array defines the selection, and the existing primary key handles duplicate inserts. The opposite-action ordering tradeoff remains the one documented for the current-state table. ### Skipped files and operational failures After the existing stable-file checks, classify zero-byte sources as informational skips. Show their filenames and reasons in Processing without a map review notice. Process them again when their contents change. Skipped describes an outcome; severity determines whether review is needed. Do not silently classify damaged or unsupported contents, parsing failures, or files without usable GPS observations as acceptable. Record their structured reason, show the issue once, and allow acknowledgement. Keep pattern exclusions distinct from content-based skips. Do not reuse EXCLUDED for both meanings. Keep any retained data from an earlier source revision identified as earlier data; acknowledging or skipping its replacement does not establish a successful current import. Job and Google Health failures retain their operational progress, retries, and recovery actions in Processing. Offline, unavailable-status, preparation, and stale-map indicators remain separate from accepted source problems. A file acknowledgement must not hide a current service failure. ### Implementation sequence Implement the common backend model first, then the complete client flow. Ship the consolidated behaviour after both phases pass their checks. #### Phase one server model and APIs 1. Define the common server issue contract, typed reasons, semantic identity, normalized severity, and lifecycle. Classify source-content problems separately from unexpected processing or service failures. Keep diagnosis and attention policy on the server. 2. Add account-scoped acknowledgement persistence and APIs through the existing repository and review services, using the database design . Guard writes with source and issue revisions; support per-file, bulk, and Reopen operations. Add the snapshot and bulk array API with set-based writes and returned summaries. Use the current-state table without an acknowledgement audit trail or replay protocol. Reset shared demo acknowledgements with its data. Use normal Liquibase schema changes without legacy backfill or migration-only endpoints. 3. Connect GPS source review and media failures to the common model. Separate GPS acknowledgement from use settings and replace the old acknowledgement bookkeeping. Preserve section choices, measurement restrictions, and the existing assessment-limit policy. Populate common issues during normal imports and explicit reassessment; do not add an automatic GPS backfill. 4. Add the narrow zero-byte skip policy and accurate outcome totals. Provide pending and acknowledged summaries and list filters through the common account-aware policy. Export the live OpenAPI schema and regenerate the TypeScript client using the normal server-first workflow. Verify backend identity, lifecycle, account scope, and snapshot guards. #### Phase two client flow and cleanup 1. Update the map, Review, and Processing flows together using the generated APIs. Keep use settings separate from acknowledgement and count each source file once. Add overall, group, and per-file actions to Processing, and derive its source-related attention from pending issues. Submit each complete bulk selection once and update all summaries from the response. Serialize opposite UI actions while their request is pending; show save failures without adding automatic mutation retries. 2.
